utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Cepic, I take it in relation to the order of your remaining witnesses, you're going to do what you can to lead as many of them today as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If that means altering the order so that as many people as possible do not have to stay the weekend, that's okay by us. You make your judgement on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course by your leave the position taken by our Defence is to follow the order that we originally announced. The witnesses after Colonel Gergar are all 92 ter witnesses, so we deal with their statements, as we've already said. So we hope that if we finish with Colonel Gergar today before the end of the first session that we'll take our next witness after that, and then depending on the cross-examination, perhaps we'll finish him, say, even before the lunch break on that condition I mean. The next two witnesses are even shorter, Dr. Petkovic and Dr. Milosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That would require suggesting that you might be suggesting putting them in front of Blagojevic so that you could clear the decks more quickly. But that's a matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Since you can't predict the cross-examination of Blagojevic, unless you've discussed it with Mr. Hannis, that way at least we would know that two of your witnesses would be completed for sure; however, we'll find out later in the day. Good morning, Mr. Gergar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will continue in a moment. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you made at the outset continues to apply to the evidence until it's completed. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Gergar.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we return 5D3029. Mr. Gergar, it might be very difficult for us to orient ourselves to the map because we are really concerned about civilians more than anything else in this case. Without you helping us in respect to where, for example, the major population centres are and it's really 5D1329, and can we magnify the bottom section of that map, just a little bit more, please. Can you see just about the middle of the map where -- or the middle of that bottom section where some lines join to make a sort of elongated oval? Do you see some writing there?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could it please be moved a bit to the left, I mean the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, I presume you know what is. Could you not tell the witness. It's cross-examination and to make some progress -- it's a difficult map to read, but I presume you've studied it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see the broken line in the middle there indicating the line on the 15th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you see below it the writing "Vucitrn"?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot discern it exactly, but I think I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you just circle where it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now that you have identified where Vucitrn is, do you know where Gornja Sudimlja is? Have you ever heard of that town?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I've never been to Gornja Sudimlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where were your mortar units located?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mortar company was in the area of the village of Bajcina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, on your military map can you place -- can you locate it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could, but the map has to be moved closer to me, I mean enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think we have to get an IC number before we can enlarge.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be IC183, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we enlarge IC183. No I think you are going in too close now. I think you need to zoom out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you zoom out one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see to the right your general area of responsibility, without being precise, could you give us a general area then of where your mortar unit would be?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere around here. Could the map be lowered a bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The trouble with an IC exhibit, Mr. Stamp, is that's it, what you see is what you get. You can't move it up and down. If you want to do that with the map, you'll need to go back to 5D1329.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Could we do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while we are doing that, I think you said or the order for this action indicated that you were also to provide support to an artillery unit; is that correct? Did you provide support to an artillery unit?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not provide support to an artillery unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, if you could just locate the general area where your mortar unit was. Once you have identified it there, could you just mark it with an M -- no, no, could you mark it.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could you mark with an arrow the direction to which they fired, to which the mortar guns fired.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without moving that map, I have here one of your combat reports of the 2nd of May 1999, it's 5D618, Your Honours, and it refers to expenditure of ammunition and it says that they used -- you used the previous night 28, 122 THG -- sorry, 28, 122-millimetre TFG rounds, are those artillery rounds or are those mortar rounds? Are 122-millimetre rounds artillery rounds or mortar rounds?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: 122-millimetre rounds are artillery rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I don't want to move this map, but I represent to you that that is what your report says, that you also fired artillery rounds. Can you recall if you did fire artillery rounds and from where.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the report we were firing using artillery as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So where was your artillery -- can you recall where your artillery was located?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's marked here on the map, where it says "Brak 211."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Can you put a put a tick beside that where it says "Brak 211."

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay, you have circled it. And with an arrow could you indicate the general direction your artillery was firing to.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to the firing to the west, who directed the fire of your artillery? I wonder if you know what I mean. Okay, let me ask you this. When you fired -- when the artillery and the mortar units fire their guns, do they normally see the target or is the fire indirect to the extent that it lands somewhere that they directed the fire at although they can't see it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We directed fire according to the requests of the MUP unit because they came along in front of this village, I think it was called Potok, and they came across a very firm defence. So they requested our artillery support in that sector. They observed the targets and they asked us to target that particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you got the bearings for these targets from them, but your gunners would not be able to see the targets?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They could not see them but on the basis of the map they knew exactly what it was that they were targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have -- persons testified here that while they were leaving the area heading towards Vucitrn in convoys they were shelled -- that are civilians -- I mean civilians in convoys were shelled from the north. Did you as commander of your brigade hear or discover anything about civilian casualties resulting from shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I as brigade commander did not hear or discover anything about civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we give this one an IC number. I think ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC184, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The envelope you got with the order for the action and the map from the Pristina Corps commander, where you get it? Where did you go to get it or did it -- was it delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In accordance with the decision map of the Pristina Corps -- well, I got that at my command post, from a courier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, when you drew your decision map, did you make any changes or did you add anything to what was on that map?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the decision map I only deployed my own units in greater detail. I didn't change anything else in relation to the decision made by the commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in deploying your units in greater detail, did you find it necessary to meet with commanders of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met with the MUP commanders just before the action started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that before or after you prepared your decision map?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after I had prepared my decision map.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you remember who the MUP commanders were?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you name them, please?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Zivaljevic and Colonel Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These were from the PJP?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yesterday you also mentioned that within your area in the course of this action -- or I'm not -- I'm not sure exactly whether you're referring to this action so maybe I should ask you. Were there also elements of the Podujevo -- what you call the Podujevo Detachment during this operation?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is, this Podujevo Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'll get back to that. We've seen a few orders here related headed "Joint Command," and you have referred to some of them in your statement. When was the first time you became aware that that term was being used in respect to actions that the VJ would be involved in?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first learned about this on the 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I understand. Are you saying you first heard the term, the expression, "Joint Command" used in respect to VJ actions on the 22nd of March, 1999? You're probably mistaken because you referenced a document that is dated the 15th of March, 1999, and in that document the term is used. So can I ask you again: Do you recall the first time you heard use of the expression "Joint Command"?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please be given a reference for this assertion just made by Mr. Stamp concerning the document dated the 15th of March, 1999, it is the 15th of March, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure if I can find that now, but that is not necessary for the question so I'll just rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Whether you're mistaken or not, you heard about the Joint Command on the 22nd of March, 1999, first?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was that in an order or were you told about it? How did you first come to know about this term?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received an envelope which contained an order to crush and destroy the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Malo Kosovo; and when I studied that I saw this term, Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we bring up P1966.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you first saw the term "Joint Command" did you make any inquiries as to what it meant?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our rules, when a brigade commander receives an order, he is duty-bound to study the order and to try to understand the order. Then, he asks his superior about the things he didn't understand. There were some things that were unclear to me in this order, so I called the commander of the Pristina Corps and I asked him to explain them to me subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I'm asking you now to focus on "Joint Command" because the document I think which is in front of you first now is not only headed "Joint Command," but at the end it says that the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija shall command and direct all forces during combat operations for the Pristina area." So if you could just focus on that. Did you make inquiries of the Pristina Corps commander in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said a moment ago. There were some things that I found unclear, and among other things I asked the commander to explain that to me. Among other things, it was this term, Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Since I had come from another corps, that was the first time that I came across this term and I did not find it clear. So I asked the commander what this meant that is to say what it meant in the heading and also what it meant in the signature. It wasn't clear to me why this order had not been signed, and it wasn't clear to me, this command post over the Pristina Corps; and that is why I spoke to the commander so that he could explain it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did he explain to you what the term "Joint Command" referred to?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What did he tell you in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In light of the fact that I was new there, the commander told me that this was a term used from 1998 onwards and that it referred to the actions or was used for the actions that were carried out by the Yugoslav Army units and MUP, the coordinated actions. Because I had received some other documents from the Pristina Corps command that did not contain this term, "the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." He explained to me that this was a term, but also that this order was an order from the corps commander, the one that he personally made, and that it pertained to a task that was issued by the corps command. And on that occasion I also asked him why the readiness for the action was not designated. He told me that I would receive the time when the action is to be carried out at a later stage, and in the afternoon a telegram arrived giving me an addendum to the decision based on this order, where the command post was specified, the command post from which the action would be commanded, and also the time was specified for the command; and it was signed by the commander, General Lazarevic. So then everything was clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if we look at this document, P1966, and we look at page 2 of the B/C/S which is also page 2 of the English, the top of page 2 of the B/C/S and the bottom of page 2 of the English you will see the command post for the Pristina Corps would be in the Pristina Corps command building in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which paragraph would that be, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's the last line of page 2 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we must have the wrong page then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is P1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Just give us a paragraph number, I think that's easier than pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you know where the Pristina Corps command building in Pristina was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there on the 20th, in Pristina I mean, in that building, but it was empty there, the building was abandoned, there was nobody there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it then this was the reason why you were uncertain about where the command post was that was referred to in this order; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was a reason too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, did you discover where the command post of the Pristina Corps was after you spoke to the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to the commander on the phone, and I was unable to ascertain where the command post was. I was told that it was in the Pristina sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. And you said that you received an addendum --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And could we bring up P1967 dated the same day, the 22nd of March, which clarified where the command post for the Pristina Corps was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall where in that document that was clarified -- or may I ask you this. Where was the command post for the Pristina Corps designated?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command post for the Pristina Corps was in the Pristina sector, and for this action the commander told me that a group of officers from the Pristina Corps would come to the Lausa sector and would exercise control over this action from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I take it then that the second order in respect to that action did not designate Lausa to be the command centre of the Pristina Corps; you were told this by the commander?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the commander told me verbally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If we -- if I may just get back to something quickly. If we look at page 8, line 15, from yesterday I think -- no, it's now page 21504, lines 16 to 18, in response to a question from learned counsel you said -- or maybe -- I'll just read the question as well. "Q. Do you recall what Ministry of the Interior forces were in the second half of April 1999 within your zone of responsibility and the 354th Infantry Brigade that you have also testified about here today?" And your answer was: "Yes, within the zone of responsibility of the 211th Armoured Brigade there were MUP forces, meaning PJP forces, and the Podujevo Detachment." That is what is recorded here as you say. You having said what's -- is that a mistake or is there such a detachment?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no such detachment. It is a section of the Podujevo interior ministry, the Podujevo OUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Were they involved in the action from 25th of April to 2nd/3rd May, the Bajgora action?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did participate in this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Earlier in your testimony you indicated that by virtue of the Law on Defence an officer of the VJ of the rank of battalion commander could designate or give duties to unarmed civilians. I would like to ask you a couple of questions about armed civilians. Are you familiar with the term the armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And while -- could we have 1975 up again I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that term, armed non-Siptar population?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received the interpretation: Armed non-Siptar population, and that's not a term that I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If you look again at this order --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if we could go to -- if you look at page 1 paragraph 2, and paragraph 2 page 1 on the English version is at page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said the Pristina Corps assignment was a Pristina Corps together with reinforcements and armed non-Siptar residents of Kosovo and Metohija support the MUP forces in defeating and destroying Albanian terrorist forces. You recall seeing that in the order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did see this in the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And if you look towards the bottom, the last section of paragraph -- of section 2, you will also see the sentence: "Armed local non-Albanians are to be assigned with guarding military facilities and roads and with protecting and defending local non-Albanians." So I think you will agree with me that this order enabled commanders of Pristina Corps units to give assignments to armed local non-Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was this possibility pursuant to the task of the Pristina Corps to issue tasks to armed non-Siptar population to secure certain facilities or features and roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And we know that there were many convoys of civilians on these roads -- well, that is not a question. I withdraw that. In your experience in Kosovo during the war, did you have any occasion to give assignments to armed local non-Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my area of responsibility I did not have an opportunity to issue any tasks to the armed non-Siptar population or to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How many were there in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my area of responsibility, there were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did your area of responsibility not include Podujevo and the villages and hamlets in the environs of Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My area of responsibility covered all that; but as for the armed non-Siptar population, there were no such persons there in my area and there was no need for me to use them to secure any facilities or the non-Siptar population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have nothing more for this witness, may it please you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gergar, do you have a hard copy of your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at paragraph 33. There's a reference to 11 of the brigade being killed and 12 wounded in terrorist and NATO attacks, and then a statement that in the zone of responsibility over 70 were killed and around a hundred were wounded. What's the difference between these two sentences?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a result of terrorist and NATO attacks, 11 members of the 211th Brigade were killed and 12 were wounded. It's a reference only to the 211th Brigade, and in the area of responsibility where the brigade had set up the defence, that would include the built-up areas, there were more than 70 people who were killed and around a hundred who were wounded. That's a reference both to the personnel and the population and also to the bus that was hit at the bridge near the village of Luzane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that's a bus hit in a NATO air-strike?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic, re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the decision map 5D1329 on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, in the section -- well, we can see the map in front of us. What was the task that the 211th Brigade was given, or rather, the elements of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The element of the 211th Armoured Brigade was given the chief task of blockading the Siptar terrorist forces, and also to provide support to MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your forces move around in this action? Did they move further than the red lines that we can see here on the right-hand side of this map?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, given that the 211th Armoured Brigade had the armour and since the NATO planes were very active at the time, the units did not move around, they remained in their sectors and that's where they set up and maintained the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just a moment, may I just intervene here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sometimes it's very difficult to object, and I don't want to be objecting unnecessarily, but the last two questions I don't think they arise from the cross-examination. They are matters which to some degree were covered in chief and in his statement, and so perhaps counsel could preface his questions by relating them to the issues that arise in cross-examination because sometimes the answers begin before one can even rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic, you can take account of that, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am referring to the questions that my learned colleague Mr. Stamp did ask and he, in fact, asked the witness to make markings on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I am a layperson as far as military matters are concerned. Could you please tell me what are the wedges and what are the lines -- or let me be more specific. Who engaged in active operations and who held passive positions?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units that were maintaining the blockade held passive positions. These are the red lines. Now, as for the active operations, the units that are marked with the green wedges are the ones that were engaged in active operations. In this case it was the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, who was in command of your forces?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The forces of the 211th Brigade were under my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the Pristina Corps command and to General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you exercise any kind of command or did you have any planning activities or any other activities that would go beyond providing support to the MUP forces? Were you in command of their forces or did you plan anything as far as they were concerned, for them I mean?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have 6D709.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague Mr. Ivetic showed this document yesterday. He showed it the other way around in the order that was not the order of the dates, but I will now follow the order of the dates. While we're waiting for this order to come up, perhaps you remember it from yesterday. This was an order where your unit was issued a task and it is indicated here that you were supposed to operate together with the MUP forces and that they were to be placed under your command. Is this how it was in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In actual fact this never happened. Every commander was in command of his unit. I was in command of the units of the 211th Brigade and the MUP was in command of its units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please just give us the date of this order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 22nd of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: To be quite specific, what was the task that you were given in this action?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this action it was our task to blockade and to prevent the spillover of the Siptar terrorist forces towards the Bajgora sector and the Malo Kosovo sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And as far as MUP was concerned, did you have any tasks related to them or was there anything else that you did?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as regards the MUP, we were supposed to provide support to them of a certain kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now have 5D1070.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This was another document that was shown to you by my colleague Mr. Ivetic. While we're waiting for this document -- okay, I can see that it's coming up. Would you please look at the date on this document.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 25th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at item 2.1. Does this confirm what you've just told us?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Since we don't have the English translation, could you please read the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The brigade units have their chief employment to support the MUP and SAJ forces in the routing and destruction of the Siptar terrorist forces in the broader sector of the Palatna village, and with an element of their forces they are to block the Siptar terrorist forces and to prevent them from pulling out of the Bajgora and Malo Kosovo area."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now look at the next page in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you the same question that Mr. Ivetic asked you about this sentence because there is something that is still not clear to me. While we're waiting for this to come up, could you please tell us whether this is your combat report, is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, that's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Item number 6, command and communications, who do you exercise command over and where is the command exercised successfully?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The communications towards or communications with the superior command and the subordinate units are functioning and they ensure successful exercise of command. NATO forces are jamming the communications intensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And who are your subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subordinates are my battalion commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague Mr. Stamp a little bit earlier indicated a page of yesterday's transcript, 2104 [as interpreted] that has to do with the question of my learned friend Mr. Ivetic, where you said that in your area there were units of the PJP in Podujevo -- of the OUP Podujevo, and I'm interested in your area. Who was in charge of law and order?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the brigade had the MUP in charge of law and order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the transcript reference was 21504.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we look at document 5D595.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This document was shown to you also by my colleague Mr. Ivetic. While we're waiting for the document, Colonel, you as a military senior officer, did you have any authority in any other structure outside of the Army of Yugoslavia in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was just carrying out the assignments that I received from my superior that had to do with organizing the defence and anti-assault combat. I didn't have any other duties in respect of the organization of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at paragraph 10 of the document and I believe we also have it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Colonel, my colleague Mr. Ivetic asked you to read paragraph 10 which says -- can you please read it because we still don't have the English on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If he's read it already, it does not need to be read again. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, my colleague Mr. Ivetic showed you this paragraph yesterday. To who does this provision apply?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This provision applies to the Army of Yugoslavia or to the members of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to go on. In respect of paragraph 32 of your statement my colleague Mr. Ivetic asked you about the difference between "rukovoditi" and "komandovati." What I'm interested in is who commanded your units and the units of the 354th Infantry Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that question. The answer is set out in the statement. This is to clarify things that are unclear; that's the sole purpose of re-examination. Now, he said in his evidence - and it says in the statement - that Colonel Nikolic and Major Djordjevic commanded the VJ forces. Are you suggesting something different?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but my colleague Mr. Ivetic suggested something else and that is why I'm putting this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's not a witness; this is the witness. It's what he says that matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not wish to leave any doubts in respect of what the witness has said and this is the reason I wish to put this question. If you permit me, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not with that question. Move to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 5D591, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Ivetic, showed you this document. Colonel, to whom does this act refer?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This act refers to the procedure of the unit if a volunteer should apply in the area of responsibility, meaning that the volunteer would have an interview and then would be sent to Kosovo Polje in order to be deployed among the ranks of the Pristina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And where did the volunteers that came to your unit come from?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The volunteers came from Nis and Belgrade, from the Bubanj Potok and Medja reception centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at P2809. My colleague Mr. Ivetic also showed you this document and put some questions to you in relation to this document. Colonel, yesterday questions were put to you regarding this document. Can you please look at it. You said that you were not able to see it clearly. What would an act like this represent according to you, if you can say that; if not, let us move on?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember the document from that time, but now that I'm reading it, it explains more to me where the MUP units were and which MUP units were in the area of responsibility of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague Mr. Stamp asked you about the arrival of the unit in the Kosovo and Metohija area in March. Can you please tell me what assignments you had and why you came to that area.

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that there was a certain degree of regression in relation to Yugoslavia already and that in the area of Macedonia NATO forces were already grouping, it was decided that the 211th Tactical Group should go to the Kosovo area in the Batlava sector for additional training and possible engagement in the event of an air-borne assault in this area. So the brigade in this period went through combat training and was in readiness for combat against air-borne assaults.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to put some questions to you about the engagement of forces in Podujevo. Can you please tell us whether these units were periodically relieved, and you were already asked questions on this by Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that they did, but I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you have precise information in the brigade about the deployment of MUP forces in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one in the brigade knew precise information about the MUP deployment in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the uniforms that the MUP members wore throughout that whole period?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this comes out of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does it arise, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify the things that Mr. Ivetic put to the witness regarding MUP, perhaps a lot of things will be clarified in the course of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What things that he put?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He asked him about the deployment of forces. He showed him charts where they were deployed, in which area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, he asked him about the deployment of MUP units in the Podujevo area; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I asked him about the deployment of MUP units in Podujevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, very well. Well, it does arise out of that. Please continue, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can you please answer my question, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had multi-coloured uniforms, somewhat similar to ours in the army, but I think they were a little bit paler and lighter and more yellow or brown colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did they have armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them did have armoured vehicles, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what was the colour of the armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIHAJLO GERGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were blue ones and also greenish ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And just one more question arising from questions put by my colleague Mr. Stamp relating to opening of fire. You marked the map. What I'm interested in is this. In organizing the fire support for the MUP, did the mortar unit or the support unit set up observation points closer to the MUP that would be supported in the course of the action and which, if necessary, would observe the fire?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't answer that question. That's a blatantly leading question. This is re-examination and that should have been an open question about where they were located. Deal with something else now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions, and I know that time is very precious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gergar, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, who is the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djura Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's Blagojevic, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Cepic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Finally we have a prosecutor in the witness-stand, Mr. Blagojevic. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, can you please tell me your full name.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Djura Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide a statement to General Lazarevic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, if I were to put the same questions to you now that were put to you when you were providing your statement, would you answer them in the same way?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Wholly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to provide a copy of the statement to the witness. [In English] Could I ask Mr. Usher just to pass one copy of statement to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Exhibit number, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like the statement to be tendered under this number, and that is 5D1402.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, sir, you explained a lot of that in your statement, but I would like to put some questions to you. What sort of indictment documents exist in our legal system?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There are the following indictment document, the indictment bill is submitted when the perpetrator is subject to a prison sentence up to three years. So this indictment bill can be issued on the basis of a criminal charge. Of course if there is evidence on a founded suspicion that the crime was committed or if the prosecution submits a proposal before a court for certain investigative actions to be conducted, and after which the person is charged. This is one of the indictment acts. There's also the so-called indirect indictment for which --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Direct indictment, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for which it is not required to have a bill, and this is for sentences of prison of up to five years. According to the criminal law, previous one and the one that is in force currently, there is the option for the prosecutor, in this case a military prosecutor, can submit to the court a proposal for no investigation to be carried out, in which case the court is obliged to interview the person to make sure that an investigation is not necessary. And if that is the finding of the court, then within eight days the prosecutor is obliged to issue an indictment. This is for crimes subject to ten years of imprisonment. And there is also an indictment after an investigation is carried out, this applies to all criminal acts, with the following remark. If indictments are always submitted, if there is founded suspicion but in a small number of cases -- unless -- with the exception of a small number of cases an investigation is always carried out before a person is charged with a crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the position where the crime is punishable with a sentence of more than ten years, which is the sort of thing that would interest us more than the other ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Crimes punishable with a sentence of more than ten years - and I have to explain it like this - there -- up to the war in our legal system there were -- because we had a complex state, in the legal terms, it was a federation, so there are federal and republican laws. The federal laws applied to the SFRY and republican laws applied in the -- and it was the republican Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia. So there were two provisions, two criminal laws, which regulated this matter differently. They were not in collision, but each in their own field stipulated punishments for certain crimes. As for the federal law, I would say that the most serious criminal acts were the crimes of -- war crimes, genocide, crimes against the constitutional order, which is a very important chapter for us, and we did have such crimes during the war. As for crimes that were -- such as murders, bodily harm, crimes against property, this was regulated by the republican criminal laws. There are also some other crimes subject to this jurisdiction, with the remark that there was special regulations guiding crimes against -- of office or duties --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if I could stop you. My question is not about that. My question's really based on a failure to understand why your statement only deals with the procedure, the indictment procedure for cases where the sentence is up to ten years. And I wonder if there's a significant difference in relation to procedure in 1999 in relation to military court procedure where the case involved a potential sentence of more than ten years, which many of the cases would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me, Your Honour, if it's a longer sentence I explained that an investigation had to be carried out because it's a more serious crime. And as far as the actual procedural part is concerned with the declaration of the state of war, a special decree was adopted in relation to the criminal code in order for the procedure to be conducted more efficiently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Cepic, this is very confusing. It would take hours to try to clarify it if you're going to ask a witness to explain it. Is it not set out in codes which are available to us so that we can read them and follow them for ourselves? We're used to reading criminal procedure provisions. It should be the simplest thing on earth to have all this documented for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you permit me, in the dossier of this case I think P1824, if I am not mistaken, is the Law on Criminal Procedure, the ZKP, that is our procedural law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is that the federal law or the republic -- it's the federal law?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. [In English] Federal law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And is it the law that applied in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue -- I note, by the way, that there are no exhibit numbers given in your -- in this witness's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, we have been discussing different types of indictments and indictment documents. Tell us, we heard another piece of testimony in this courtroom earlier that around 1.000 persons or 900 persons had indictments issued against them. Do you perhaps know what the distinction is, what the percentage of these persons related to indictments that were issued after an investigation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: About 500, 600, that would be the tentative figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have no idea what that is about, Mr. Cepic, none at all. We were confused with the witness who dealt with it before, and the answer we've just had is meaningless.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be permitted to clarify the matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've no option if you want us to take account of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Prosecutor, could you please be as brief and as concise as possible in your answers, and I'll do my best to put questions that are like that. For what crimes was an investigation carried out? Give us the exact crimes.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: During the course of the war you mean? I cannot mention all of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The most frequent ones.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the most serious crimes, first of all, in the office of the prosecutor where I was the prosecutor it was the crime of espionage, where there was an investigation carried out in view of one case and it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down and not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, overlap, and the interpreter has been unable to interpret any of your question so far. You'll need to observe a pause after the witness completes his answer and before you begin your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As a matter of fact, I'm looking at the clock more than at the witness in order to speed things up, but of course I'm going to comply with your instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, tell me, what were the most frequently committed crimes for which an investigation was carried out?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: All the crimes envisaging sentences over five years' of imprisonment were those that were the most frequently investigated ones, and after that the office of the prosecutor would make its own decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please give me a few examples.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The crimes against the constitutional order, like espionage, there are two crimes; then there were crimes against life and limb, serious injuries; and all crimes against the Army of Yugoslavia that dominated, if I can put it that way, in these proceedings, from Article 211, not carrying out an order, not answering a call-up, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in war crimes here, homicide, robbery, theft, disappropriation of motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can say that in both offices of the prosecutor, and bearing in mind the fact that the total number of criminal reports were 2.382, almost a fifth relates to those particular crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Who could file a criminal report?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the filing of criminal reports, first of all let me explain that in most cases this is done by the military police and the security organs, but also any person, any citizen, rather, a soldier, a commander of a unit, et cetera, anyone formally and legally is able to file a criminal complaint. May I repeat once again? 95 per cent of the cases have to do with the military police making such -- filing such reports, and these are of higher quality than other ones. In case a citizen directly files a criminal complaint, then it is the duty of the prosecutor to deal with that. It can be in writing, but if it is done verbally then it is the prosecutor's duty to compile a note about that report to check things out, and then take measures in order to prosecute the perpetrator of the crime, or rather, he requires additional information about what had happened and then makes a decision. Another thing I'd like to note. From a formal and legal point of view, it doesn't only matter to have a report filed. If the prosecutor hears that someone had committed a crime, then the prosecutor himself takes action, of course through the organs of the SUP, or rather, the military police, takes measures in order to have the perpetrator prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could citizens file such reports?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I said a few moments ago, if I said anyone, then no one's excluded, any person can file a criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The thing I would like a clear answer to here, rather than all the minute detail, is the circumstances in which an investigating judge has to be brought in to carry out an investigation and then make a recommendation to the prosecutor on the action to be taken. Can you give me a simple answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When something happens, something that constitutes a crime, that is to say if the military police learns of something like that, they inform the prosecutor about that and the investigative judge. If it is necessary to have an on-site investigation carried out, then the investigating judge comes to the site and also the prosecutor. It is the duty of the judge to carry out an on-site investigation and to write-up a document on this, and then this document is submitted to the prosecutor in order to prosecute the said person. And also, that is how a prosecutor's decision is made ultimately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But if the complaint is of looting or theft from someone of his documents or money, something of that nature, is there an investigation carried out by an investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether he'll carry out an investigation primarily depends on the prosecutor who asks for an investigation. If the prosecutor has sufficient evidence, meaning that it is not necessary to carry out an investigation, then the investigation will not be carried out. If there is not enough evidence, then an investigation will be carried out, and then the prosecutor is going to decide whether he is going to bring charges against such a person or will give up on the prosecution or will perhaps extend the charges in order to include other people if there is sufficient evidence, that is. I do apologise, I would like to say something else, Mr. President. Perhaps - how should I put this? - we are dealing with common law and civil law and there is a major difference involved, and I am trying to explain this to the best of my ability. The role of the prosecutor and of the investigating judge are quite different in terms of criminal prosecution when compared to Anglo-Saxon law. So it is really the prosecutor that has to take action, and the court can only do what is prescribed by law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what you've just said then, what is the relevance of whether the sentence is up to three years, whether the sentence is up to five years, whether it's up to ten years or more? What's -- what is that distinction that you're trying to make in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sentence is very important, the sentence envisaged is very important for prosecuting crimes. It makes it possible for the prosecutor to deal as quickly as possible with less serious crimes, and as far as very serious crimes are concerned entailing ten-year prison sentences, et cetera, to have an investigation carried out and then a decision is made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] With your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems to me we'll just have to read this for ourselves in the light of what's been said to us, and you should get on to something more specific. If you have any more questions for the witness, and we can get to cross-examination and then see if what needs to be clarified in re-examination after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. By your leave may I just clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just give me an example of separate maximums. What are separate maximums? What crimes entail a prison sentence of up to three years?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Up to three years, less-serious crimes. For example --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For example, let's say theft, looting, what kind of theft?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, theft is five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What about aggravated robbery?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Aggravated robbery, ten years, but then there is also petty theft, and that is up to three years. That is Article 173. And if somebody committed petty theft, then -- can I explain once again how it is that the indictment bill can be issued? But then when there is a case of aggravated theft involving up to ten years in prison, then an investigation has to be carried out. That is why it is so important what the envisaged sentence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honours, should I clarify this further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the answer is, as I've said, that we will read it and we will be able to follow the system better I think by reading the procedural documents. In any event, what really matters is what action was taken in the circumstances that prevailed at the time. That's what we really want to concentrate on, rather than get bogged down in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'd like to deal with specific examples now. Mr. Blagojevic, are you aware of what happened in Pusto Selo and Senovac and the mass grave that was found there?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard of this; however, I as a prosecutor and my deputies also, we did not take measures as envisaged by law in these cases. But I know that this incident - how should I put this? - on the basis of the decision of the prosecutor was not dealt with by a military court; it was dealt with by the district court in Pristina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Prizren, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I think Dobrivoj Peric dealt with this case because the perpetrators of this crime were not military persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this referred to in the statement, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. It's relatively late when the statement arrived here, I mean, so we did not have enough time to deal with some questions additionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, do you know Lakic Djorovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you work with him?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in the proceedings against him?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As for the criminal proceedings against this person, they are underway. I am a witness in these proceedings and the principle is not to speak of cases that are underway, then I rather wouldn't but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement you already refer to that, but I'm just asking about whether this is still an active case against Lakic Djorovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge the proceedings were initiated before the court in Nis with respect to three crimes -- of course this happened after the war. And then after that it was delegated to the military court in Belgrade. And now, after the military courts were abolished, it's the district court in Belgrade that is dealing with it. I know that because I was summoned five or six months ago to be a witness in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Will you find a suitable time to interrupt, please, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be grateful if it's right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Blagojevic, we have to have a break at this stage for half an hour. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we shall resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, let us continue. We mentioned Lakic Djorovic. I showed him your statements, the statement that General Ojdanic's Defence uploaded into the system. It is an interview, or rather, your statement in the proceedings against him where you say that he caused general danger, that there was an incident at the Belgrade bar Railway Track, that's at pages 1169 [as interpreted] and 11680 of the transcript in that case and he said that what you said was untrue. Do you still maintain what you said?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely maintain that what I said is true, and this is the fact that I learned from him when this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Your Honours, we included in our exhibit list two documents recently. My colleague Mr. Hannis is on his feet and I know why. This is the judgement convicting Lakic Djorovic of causing grievous bodily harm to his mother-in-law, he beat her up, that's 5D1406, and we have an official note from the police confirming that this incident took place and corroborating what Witness Blagojevic said, that is 5D1407. Both these documents were received from the Prosecution in January as Rule 68 material, and I can see that my learned colleague Mr. Hannis is on his feet and that he would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, actually, I got up to speak about what I saw was an error in the transcript at page 38, line 24, there's a reference to pages 1169 and 11680, so one of those two I think must be wrong. And I also wanted a reference to this witness's statement that's an exhibit, if we can have that exhibit number for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of the exhibit is already in the transcript, that's -- anyway, the number of the exhibit is 5D1402 and the page reference is 1169 [as interpreted] and 11680 and the exhibits that I would like to tender into evidence are 5D1406 and 5D1407.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you serious about these transcript references, 116 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, you've given us them twice now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, actually I said 11679 and 11680.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you saying 5D1406 and 1407 are not already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They are in the record. We filed a motion to have them included on our list, we did that a few days ago. We did not submit a translation of those documents because we did not have it at the time. But let me repeat that once again that we received it from the Prosecution in January under Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, have you anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Well, we will mark them for identification. Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would like to note one more thing. The witness spoke about the location Pusto Selo Senovac, and we have exhibits that are already in the system indicating that necessary measures were taken by the authorised prosecutor, that's 5D127 and 5D128, these are the documents. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Any problem with these, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, the Izbica location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, how long is your examination to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Not more than ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, the location Izbica is among the charges in this case. Do you have any knowledge of a mass grave in that location?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber permits --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Be very brief, please.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Before Colonel Stanimir Radosavljevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Milosavljevic"] a military prosecutor -- actually, he received information about this incident, and the military prosecutor took the measures that were within his purview. He put this report in the file, it was filed under KR, that's miscellaneous crimes, and he conducted an investigation against the perpetrator. And once he ascertained that no military personnel were involved in the crime, he informed the district prosecutor in Kosovska Mitrovica about that case and submitted all the relevant documents to him. And I believe that this case is currently -- the proceedings are conducted before the Kosovska Mitrovica district court, but I don't have any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We heard that after the state of war was rescinded and after the personnel no longer were considered military personnel, that those cases were referred to civilian courts. I would like to know how many of those cases were actually referred to civilian courts and why was that so.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: They were referred to civilian courts because once those persons were no longer considered to be military personnel, military courts were -- no longer had the jurisdiction over those cases. And it's about 300 to 400 cases that were referred to regular courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it there is some clear rule to this effect that having had jurisdiction a court loses jurisdiction when a reservist leaves the army, and it would be helpful for us to be -- our attention to be drawn to that particular provision because it does seem an odd one at first sight.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, let me explain this in some detail. The Law on Military Courts, Articles 9 through 12 stipulate the jurisdiction, but let me explain this in brief. Article 9 states that military court can try only military personnel for all crimes. Article 10 stipulates that --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Slow down, not everything is being recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat because of the intervention of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second. We've now lost track of your answer. Go back to what you were saying about Article 10, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 10 stipulates that military courts may try civilians, that's the legal term, for the following crimes, if you allow me: That's Article 121 through 139 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and for any crimes against the Army of Yugoslavia, that's Articles 201 through 239. Can I continue about this topic of jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If accomplices in a crime are military personnel and civilians and if a regular court has jurisdiction over this civilian, then the regular court will also have jurisdiction to try the military person, the serviceman. But, if you allow me, if the civilian person is actually in the army and if such a person committed the crime in the course of performing his office, together with the civilian in that case the military court would have jurisdiction to try both these persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not addressing the problem at all here Mr. Cepic can ask about it further if he wishes, but all I was suggesting is that if as soon as possible our attention can be drawn to the rule that tells us all of this, then we'll work it out for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I quoted the relevant provisions, that's Articles 9, 10, 11, and 12 of the Law on Military Courts, they define in detail the jurisdiction of military courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the particular question is related to a single person being a military person committing a crime, and then the military court losing jurisdiction over him because he is demobilised. And it's that provision that we would like to have identified. Now, if it's somewhere in that region, we'll find it when we read the code. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, let me explain. The fact that the war has stopped and this military person is no longer -- no longer has the status of a military person, by the very fact that the war has ended, the jurisdiction of the military court no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that means the military court would not have jurisdiction over a military person either because the war is over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It absolutely does have because the military person still maintains -- retains --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And similarly, if a civilian assaults, attacks, a soldier and the military court has jurisdiction, are you suggesting it loses jurisdiction if that soldier leaves the army? It wouldn't make any sense if it did. Is there such a rule as well, that if the status of the victim changes the court also loses jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a hypothetical question and the only answer I can give you is the following. If a civilian commits a crime - and I've already quoted the relevant articles and described the crimes - the military court has absolute jurisdiction and no other fact can wrest this jurisdiction away from the military court. But if a military person loses this status, then as stipulated in the relevant articles of the Law on Military Courts that I just quoted, this is what happens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that seems to be the interpretation that's been followed, but that will be a matter for us to consider. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: During the war did you also prosecute terrorists?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and let me clarify, if I may. One of the gravest crimes under our law is terrorist acts and conspiracy to commit hostile action, and that is punishable under Article 139. In the year 1998 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, we have lots of this information in your statement. I was very specific in my question. I'm interested in the war. Were any terrorists prosecuted during the war?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and the cases where the perpetrators were unknown were also dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we already have a system, 4D509, it's in the system, and it deals with the perpetrators of terrorist acts who had been identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
