utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, was anyone able to exert any influence over the work of the military prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely and strenuously deny that anybody could influence the work of the military prosecutors and the decision-making process, the decisions that military prosecutors had to take under the law. If anything of the sort happened, nothing like that happened, but the military prosecutor had the power to actually prosecute the person responsible for that. That could be classed as incitement to abuse office. So the prosecutor had the power to prosecute such a person to prevent any such kind of influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And what would happen if General Lazarevic were to influence you?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know in what sense he could actually do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you have done had he tried to influence you?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've just told you, I could have taken legal measures, I could have prosecuted him, I could have reported him through the police, I could have instigated criminal proceedings, I could have referred that to my senior military prosecutor, Colonel Radosavljevic, and he then had the power to file a report higher up the chain of command and proceedings would have been instituted because it is stipulated by law that military prosecutors are to be independent and the Law on Military Prosecutor's Office stipulate in which way military prosecutors are to go about their business, of course always applying the relevant provisions of the Law on Criminal Procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I have just two more questions. Did you send reports on your work to other addressees?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the war and after the war, reports were sent first to the higher military prosecutor's office and then also to the commands. I think that if you have any of my memos you will see that this was the command of the military district.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. While you're talking could we please have 3D533, the last page on our screens, and then you can continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: So the Pristina Military District command, the Pristina Corps command, the 3rd Army command, that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Could we have on our screens 3D533, please. [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one more directive while we're waiting for the document. In his statement in several paragraphs the witness referred to the book: "Application of International Law of War" by author Ivan Markovic, and that is Exhibit P1011.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, do you recognise your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment, I do recognise it. It is my signature; that is not in dispute, but I believe that on the last page of my report it does state to which organs the report was sent. This is only the statistical part of the report with statistical data. I would like to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can look at page 2 or 3 in the B/C/S. The next page, please, in the B/C/S. And the following page. And the following page. Page 6 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a brief question. Why is the document being given to all of these bodies?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: According to the military prosecutor in order to monitor crimes, and as for units this is a guide-line for the units to monitor disciplinary and other measures for the purpose of imposing discipline. I'm not quite familiar with how it works there, but it is our duty to provide them with an overview of crimes that are under the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And now my last question. I asked you this when we were speaking of yesterday. Did you prosecute Colonel Vlatko Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Should I --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, just tell us in one sentence why.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't recollect exactly the time when this was, but I do remember that it was a crime of falsifying an official document. And I think, but I'm not sure, that the proceedings against him were initiated during the investigation. It seems to me that first he was a witness, and then he was interrogated as an accused. And it's about falsifying a document. It's a lighter crime. There is no gain from the crime, but it has to do with entering incorrect or untrue data into an unofficial document. I think he did that through incitement. He's not the direct perpetrator, but incited the act to be done, which means that he either made the decision or helped for the person who actually perpetrated the crime to make this decision or incited the person to commit that. Why is this a less-grave crime? I think the sentence passed on him was a suspended sentence and I think there -- and I think we did not appeal that decision. We were satisfied with the decision. And I would like to state one more thing. As for that accused, it was my impression that he acted very honourably in confessing the crime because we didn't have any other evidence. Had he not done that, we would not have had any evidence against him, so that is why I believe that in this case he behaved honourably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the basis for instigating the proceedings if there was no evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you followed me. The charges were against other persons, but in the course of the investigation he made his confession, first of all as a witness, and then subsequently he was questioned as an accused, in the capacity of an accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who are the others that you were investigating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there were two professional soldiers or members of the military, but perhaps if you showed me the document I will be able to remember better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who reported it to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police probably. I don't believe that it was someone else. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't you have the basic information who reported it, who was being investigated? No?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I can answer that question if I look at the particular case, the document, but I cannot remember it just like that. It was probably done by the police because this is something that was committed by the professional cadre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in preparing for today were you asked to explain your opinion of the role of Vukovic as an honourable role?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I emphasised this on a number of occasions in conversation, and after that I also met the person so there is no influence in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why did you feel the need to tell us that today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I feel the need for a number of reasons. When in such proceedings it happens that charges are issued in such a way, it's a special procedure and you know that perpetrators usually conceal their acts, they do not speak the truth, and so on and so forth. So this is a case unlike [Realtime transcript read in error "like"] that, so I felt that I needed to mention that particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which do you think is more serious, being the officer who tells a soldier to falsify a record or being the soldier who falsifies the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, naturally it's more serious when it's something that's done by an officer, but I really cannot go into that now unless I see the dossier, whether it's a conscript, a regular soldier, or an officer that is involved, then there is a difference there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. I would just like to make a correction in the transcript. On page 50, line 1, the witness said that he did -- is not such a case, and here we have a completely different meaning. That part of his answer is missing or perhaps we can listen to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to be useful, Your Honours, 1309 is the Law on Military Courts and the Court can look at Article 13, paragraph 1, where the question of jurisdiction is explained on which you put questions to the witness. That's what I wanted. That was one thing. The other thing is that I know that we are short on time, so if Mr. Hannis would like to question the witness about crimes for which a death sentence is stipulated and about perpetrators, then I would not -- I would not have to question the witness. But if he is not going to do that, then I will be the one to put these questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume Mr. Fila should proceed, Mr. Hannis. Yes, please proceed with your questions, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask you something. You know that we were a bit troubled, and this is something that is not easy to understand for other people. During the examination-in-chief by Mr. Cepic, you said that the gravest crimes were covered in a special section of the KPZ of the federal law and that other crimes, not-so-serious crimes were covered by the republican law; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now, can you explain how it came about that in 1999 we have the death sentence for murder, according to the republican Serbian law, and there is no sentence or punishment for genocide. Or to put it this way: Under the assumption that I carry out a genocide and kill off a whole people, what is the sentence that I would be subject to and what would be the sentence if I were to kill a soldier and steal 100 dinars from his pocket? We're talking about 1999. And where does this absurd situation come from?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you permit me, may I answer? Your Honours, may I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this, the collision and the legal mess with these laws is something that we had to face with. In 1996 under political influences provisions of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia [as interpreted] were changed because the death sentence was abolished. Instead of the death sentence, the most serious sentence prescribed by a sentence of imprisonment of up to 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Which law? It was wrongly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The criminal law of the SFRY --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the FRY, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but the Assembly did not wish to change the laws of the Republic of Serbia. So all of these provisions regarding crimes remained the way they were in the republican law and the death sentence and most serious sentences remaining, but here it has been reduced, so we had a dual situation in respect to these provisions. So for such grave crimes the federal law had milder sentences than the republican law, and this created major problems in the application of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that the sentence for genocide would be 15 years; and were he to kill a policeman who caught him in the perpetration of a crime, he would be sentenced to death?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Because this would be aggravated murder under Article 47, which covers the murder of a military person or a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is just proof that politicians should not be allowed to meddle with the law and meddle with what they don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now another question that is also very important for this court is this: Can you please explain, but briefly, we don't have a lot of time, what is the duty of reporting a crime? When you see somebody committing a crime that has to be prosecuted, is every citizen obliged to report this crime and what sentence would he be subject to were he not to report that crime? Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. In Article 199 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and according to Article 203 of the law of the Republic of Serbia, failing to report a crime is -- I will now paraphrase the provisions that I mentioned and they are: If a person knows about someone who perpetrated a grave crime subject to a sentence of 40 years' imprisonment, they would be punished by a sentence of imprisonment of up to three years. If he knows that a crime was committed but is not aware of the perpetrator but fails to report it, he will also be subject to a three-year sentence of imprisonment. An official who deliberately fails to report a crime that he becomes aware of while performing his duties subject to the same punishment, and there's also another important provision if we're talking about the spouses or relatives, they are privileged in the sense that they will not be prosecuted if they do not report that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Just one thing I failed to mention that we're talking about 1999 when the death sentence was still in force and in the other side it was 15 years.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've missed an answer, Mr. Fila. You said: "Just one thing I failed to mention that we're talking about 1999 when the death sentence was still in force and in the other side it was 15 years." Now, what did you say in response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does your answer relate -- refer to 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 1999, the most -- and it refers to the most serious of crimes. That's the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for taking time, but I think that it was useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Ivetic, what's your interest in this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Cross-examination on two paragraphs of the statement and the matter that was brought up with respect to the criminal report on Izbica. So seven or eight questions all total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir, my name is Dan Ivetic and I'm one of the attorneys for Sreten Lukic, and as I indicated I will just have a handful of questions for you. If we can look at paragraph 29 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's Exhibit 5D1402, page 4 of both the English and the Serbian. And could you clarify for me in paragraph 29, are you talking about civilian or military prosecutors and in what context are you referring to the internal affairs organs?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am speaking only about the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor, and it is just paraphrased here, but we're talking about the military police here so there's just the confusion with the word "internal affairs" here. If you permit me, I would just like to clarify. It's a provision, like I said before, the provision that has the force of a decree, meaning that the military prosecutor can conduct an investigation. I don't know if there was such a case that any prosecutor actually conducted an investigation in the course of the war, but that is the sense of the decree law.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I apologise. We had to wait for the transcript and the translation. Thank you for clearing that up for me. Moving on to paragraph 69 of your statement, which is page 12 in the English, the second-to-last page in the Serbian original. You cite some kind of commission relating to the Istok municipality. Do you recall that if in that commission there were any MUP representatives?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the names. I think you can see that from the report, but I really -- I'm unable to remember that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Fair enough. Do you recall if the MUP representatives participated in drafting the eventual report that you just made reference to?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you permit me, I would like to answer the question. I did not take part in drafting of the report because that was not part of my duties. If a crime occurred, then the judge and the prosecutor carry out their legal duties. As for the report, that is a matter for other organs. I did not have any part in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: And if you permit me, just in relation to that event --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... We have time constraints here, and I have a very limited interest in this, and I think I can dispose of it with one more question. Do you agree with me or do you know that the MUP members of the commission did not participate in the drafting of the final report and did not sign off on the same, given that it was only signed by Colonel Djakovic of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot really say anything about the report because it is not part of my legal duties to draft reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now if we could move along to my last item which Mr. Cepic, my colleague, asked you about, Izbica. Just to be clear, before I start asking questions, when you talk about the reporting of that incident are we talking about the criminal denunciation sent by the security organs of the VJ to the military prosecutor of the Pristina Corps on the 29th of May, 1999, number KR2900 regarding the suspected criminal act of murder relating to the discovery of 144 fresh graves in the village of Izbica? Is that the incident or event that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Allow me just to explain. I was not a prosecutor in that case and I cannot speak about it, but I know I heard of this incident and I've already said that if something like that happens, what the prosecutor is supposed to do is to first of all see what kind of a crime is involved, whether there are --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: -- some perpetrators who are known in order to see whether he has jurisdiction to act. However, Stanimir Milosavljevic [sic] informed me that he had taken all measures, asked for information about the incident and who the possible perpetrators could be. When they came to the conclusion that these incidents had nothing to do with military personnel, then it was the local prosecutor's office that dealt with it in Kosovska Mitrovica. I think that was in 2001, I think that was it. I think that that is when he wrote to that prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did the military prosecutor Mr. Milosavljevic [sic] undertake an actual investigation into the matter before transferring it to the civilian courts; and if so, where can we find that documentation? [Interpretation] Was an investigation carried out?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to say this: How --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note we could not hear the speaker. Other microphones seem to be on or Mr. Ivetic's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on please. The interpreters seem to be having difficulty hearing what you're saying, so could you start that answer again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Please repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, if you would speak one language things would be simpler for all concerned. Please answer. I'm sorry, what is it you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [In English] Pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you said something.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, there was no investigation in this case because the perpetrator was unknown. If the perpetrator is unknown, then the investigation cannot be carried out. This is an incident that was registered as miscellaneous crimes, KR, I explained that, in the prosecutor's office. And when sufficient information is compiled, then an investigation can start, but it is only against military personnel that the prosecutor's office acts, the military prosecutor's office. However, since this case was referred to the local prosecutor's office in Kosovska Mitrovica, then the military prosecutor's office no longer had jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the Court's leave, that was my final question for this witness. If Your Honours wish to explore further, by all means, otherwise I pass the witness to Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just want to follow-up on that last answer you gave. You said: "If the perpetrator is unknown, then the investigation cannot be carried out ..." That seems backwards to me. Don't you have to do some investigation first to see if you can find out who the perpetrator is?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure states that an investigation is carried out against a particular person, that is to say that the perpetrator has to be known. You are probably referring to the collection of necessary information that in our law, in civil law, is considered to be what you term "investigation."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess that's right. I'm using the word "investigate" in the sense of gathering information to try and find out what happened and who did it.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in connection with that you said at page 55, line 8, today you said regarding Izbica that no military prosecutor -- well, actually, it was -- I'm sorry. Mr. Ivetic asked you about paragraph 29 of your statement, and in your answer you said no military -- as far as you recall "no military prosecutor investigated." So I guess what you mean is you're using that "investigate" as a term of art because it didn't -- didn't your boss Stanimir Radosavljevic do some gathering of information before being able to reach the conclusion that the VJ was not involved in the killings of those persons at Izbica? He must have done something before he was able to reach that conclusion, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have said that when he learned of what had happened, he took all measures that he was authorised to take. After this information was gathered, he made this kind of decision. As for conducting an investigation, I'm going to repeat once again, it is only a court of law that is in charge of carrying out an investigation. This decree that was in force during the state of war states that the prosecutor can do so as well. However, I have already said that I'm not aware of any cases when a prosecutor did that, carried out an investigation, during the war. Even during the war it was the court of law that conducted investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, when you say the prosecutor took all authorised measures, what are the authorised measures he's able to do in terms of gathering information?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There are several steps involved, if I can put it that way, but mainly it has to do with the following. He should ask the organs of the military police and the military security to submit information on the incident, to interview the participants, persons who have information about the incident, if there are damaged parties, injured parties, to hear these persons, to interview them, to compile all documents on the basis of which he can make his further decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with Izbica, what can you tell us about what Radosavljevic specifically did? This was -- well, let me -- before you answer that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the name is Milosavljevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that was said a couple of times, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are right, it's a mistake, Radosavljevic, it's a mistake. It's not Milosavljevic, it is Radosavljevic. You're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You are aware that this Izbica incident was a significant incident that had international media attention around the end of May and early June 1999, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I learned of this incident after the war. I did not work at the military prosecutor's office, or rather, attached to the command of the Pristina Corps. I was the military prosecutor attached to the command of the military district, and this incident did not fall within the jurisdiction of my prosecutor's office but the prosecutor attached to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. How did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked at the military prosecutor's office Stanimir Radosavljevic was my military prosecutor, my superior officer, if I can put it that way, and this knowledge dates back to 2000 or 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you weren't aware of it before that, you didn't know that it had been on the internet and international media?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we show the witness Exhibit P2213.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before I ask you a question about this document, in paragraph 44 of your statement, the second paragraph under that number in about the middle, you explain that if a military prosecutor's office got a report on a crime committed by an organ of the MUP, the report would be forwarded to the competent municipal or district prosecutor. Did it -- did that work the other way? If MUP got a report or information that the VJ might have been involved in the crime, did they forward reports to you, to the military prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were supposed to. That is the legal procedure involved, those who are competent are supposed to take the necessary measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could look at Exhibit P2213 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I don't have an English translation of this, but it's a fairly short document. I'd like to ask the witness to read it, if that's all right with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see, sir, this is a document dated the 27th of May, 1999, in the upper left. Can you tell us who this document is coming from?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can familiarise with it and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All I'm asking you to do now is read it. You can read it, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: "Official note compiled on the 27th of May, 1999, in the offices of the crime and PD technical office. "Following the news broadcast on the internet" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, just one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm just trying to be of assistance and useful to the Trial Chamber. I think that 6D, the 6D Defence has a translation of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ivetic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 6D115, and we do have an English translation from CLSS that's in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That would be great. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you want to read the B/C/S when it's back on the screen to yourself, I can ask you a question from the English that I have now. We see this is dated the 27th of May, 1999, and it appears to be from the crime investigation police department, Kosovska Mitrovica. It's an official note and it mentions that they were investigating a news item reported on the internet about a mass grave in the village at Izbica. You'll see that the person signing apparently went there, and on the way: "We found out about the village of Izbica from VJ members we met. In the village we came upon some ten soldiers and asked them if they knew of the existence of 'mass graves.' They shrugged their shoulders, but they did point out the existence of a new graveyard." And then these people writing this official note went on down and looked at that. And you're telling me that you or your prosecutor's office didn't receive any information about that, either from the MUP or from the internet or from international media in late May or early June 1999?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I absolutely confirm that I did not receive such information. This is the first time I see this official note here in this courtroom. Colonel Stanimir Radosavljevic probably knew about this, whether he received this note and when he received it, if he received it. I cannot state my views on something that I never received.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And did the Colonel tell you what persons he might have talked to in his preliminary gathering of information to help him conclude that the VJ was not involved in the Izbica incident?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can give you the following answer. The prosecutor is my superior. He's not duty-bound to report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that --

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: -- in such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm just asking, did he?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. I have no obligation in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand you have no obligation. I'm just asking if he told you.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: He did not. This was just an informal conversation during which I found out how this report, or rather, this case was referred to the court in charge in Kosovska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me go back to your statement. When did you first join the army?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: When I completed secondary military school and that was on the 18th of July, 1980.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for how long did you remain in the army from 1980?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: From 1980 until 2004, when I went to work at the district prosecutor's office in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What rank did you hold when you left the army?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see you went to law school, you graduated in 1995, you worked as a clerk until the war broke out. What were your duties as a clerk in the legal service in the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: My duties in the Pristina Corps related to carrying out administrative procedure and taking measures in relation to military disciplinary procedure as well as obligations from the military public attorney's office, and I received my instructions from the then-attorney in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see that you were appointed military prosecutor at the Pristina Military District command. When was that, right after the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean when I was appointed military prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand. I was appointed to this duty and I assumed this office I think on the 27th of March, 1999. By a previous presidential decree I was appointed judge at the military court at the command of the Pristina Corps. For two or three days I took part in the preparations, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, prior to this you had no previous experience working as a prosecutor, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say you were appointed the military prosecutor, were you the boss? Were you the number one prosecutor in that office at the Pristina Military District command?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how many deputies did you have working under you when you were first appointed?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Djordje Aksic, Momcilo Dedic, Dragoljub Zdravkovic, and Miodrag Brkic were my deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 4 you say subsequently you were deputy military prosecutor. Does that mean did you get demoted or did somebody get appointed over you? What happened?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: As prescribed by law, by a presidential decree I was replaced, dismissed from that office, I don't know the reasons, but I assume it has to do with the fact that I rejected 492 criminal reports based on Article 214 that had to do with failure to respond to call-up. Later on this was considered to be the right decision, but I have nothing to say in relation to a presidential decision; I can just act in accordance with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who was put in your place?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Then-Lieutenant-Colonel Lakic Djorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You tell us in paragraph 5 that the military prosecutor's offices were abolished I think at the end of 2004. Is that the right date?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 31st of December, 2004. Now, why do I know? Because something happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, that's okay. Let me ask you this: Do you know why they were abolished on that date?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we understood from an earlier witness that there's no statute of limitations on war crimes. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, but there's just something I have to add. There is no statute of limitations on war crimes and genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And so now if unknown perpetrators are discovered or genocide or other war crimes are discovered, who will prosecute those cases now if the war -- if the military prosecutor's offices have been abolished? What's the provision to allow for that now?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: There is a law on the take-over of jurisdiction from military courts, military prosecutors, and military legal offices.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that law states what the military departments will be attached to courts and prosecutor's offices. There are three military departments, in Novi Sad, Belgrade, and Nis. I am the head of the military department in the district court in Nis. For your information, I am counsel for prosecution in the case against Zlatan Mancic, Radivojevic, Tosic, and Sergei who have been charged with committing war crimes. However, since this is an ongoing case I cannot say anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the date of that law. Can you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not remember the exact date, but I certainly know that it was in the year 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we move on, when you refer to your position as a deputy prosecutor -- deputy military prosecutor or deputy district public prosecutor, does that mean you are one of a number of ordinary prosecutors or does it make you number 2 in the department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not quite understand you. When I say at the military department of the district public prosecutor's office in Nis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's the word "deputy" I'm trying to be clear about. "Deputy" could mean that you stand-in for the chief or it could mean that you're just one of the other group of prosecutors at ordinary level. Which is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say this. Deputy prosecutor, that is below the military prosecutor. They have the same rights and responsibilities; however, the military prosecutor says who the first deputy is going to be, the first among equals, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you -- after you gave your statement, it's Exhibit 5D1402, I take it you had a chance to go through it and review it, make any corrections, and I see in the B/C/S it appears to be a signature and -- yeah, a signature at the bottom of each page. Is that yours?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: This one? Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to ask you in paragraph 11 you talked about: "The following bodies were established when the state of war was proclaimed on 27 March 1999." I think this -- maybe this is just a translation issue. Wasn't the state of war declared on the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It was probably a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then on the 27th, is that the date when the military court and the military prosecutor's offices were established?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what it's about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And here you mention the military court at both the Pristina Corps command and the military district command and the military prosecutor's office at the military district command, but wasn't there a prosecutor's office set up at the Pristina Corps command at the same time?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there are two prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in paragraph 16, after you've listed the various people that were appointed to these courts and prosecutor's offices, in your statement you say: "The above persons were appointed to these posts by decree of the President of the FRY of 26 March 1999 ..." Now, were they appointed to these positions before the courts and the prosecutor's offices were created on the 27th? Or are the dates just mixed up? Or do you know?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot but I assume that some time is required for a decree to arrive and to have these persons informed about that because the decree comes from Belgrade. Now, when this is going to be carried through, it probably requires some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You understand my question, though, you know, how can you appoint people to jobs or positions that haven't even been created yet?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: A state of war was declared on the 24th of March. That is to say legal conditions were created for the establishment. If it's the 26th of March, then it is only logical that it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 17 you mention the Law on Military Prosecutor's Offices, and I think as Mr. Fila helpfully told us, Your Honour, that's in Exhibit P1309. In paragraph 18 you say that "A military prosecutor may request any necessary information from the parties that filed the report." Does the military prosecutor have any authority to take action if the parties from whom he requests information either ignore or refuse such a request? Can you do anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you can do something. The authorities that do not want to implement this decision can be notified, and this is what was done in cases like that. Decisions were made or sanctions were imposed, but in practice I am not aware of a single case where the security organ or the military police would fail to comply with the orders received from the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 21 you tell us how military prosecutors are appointed, and that's during peacetime I gather. And in paragraph 26 you tell us how the process works during a state of war. And regarding that, during the state of war you say they are appointed, removed, or relieved of their duties by the president of the republic, I take it that's the republic of the FRY, Mr. Milosevic at that time, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but for our lawyers the person doesn't matter; it is the provisions that matter, the regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's done on the recommendation of the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify something. This is what is stipulated in the law, but it doesn't mean that it's an obligation. This is not an obligatory norm, but the president can do that, at least not the way I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I don't understand. Do you mean somebody else other than the president could appoint, relieve, and remove the military prosecutors and their deputies?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. What I meant was that formally and legally this proposal need not be made in writing. It can be made verbally by the chief of the Supreme Command Staff. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I take it when you say it's done on the recommendation of the Chief of Staff, that's a non-binding recommendation, right? If President Milosevic disagreed, he didn't have to follow the recommendation of the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I really can't say that. This is not within my purview. Lawyers who deal with that can do so, they -- those who are in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, what did you understand the Supreme Command to be during the state of war? What person or persons would you be referring to?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as a lawyer I really can't give you an answer to that question. That's not something that I know, and this is not something that I should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, it's in your statement. Did you put that in there or did somebody else put that in there?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: But allow me. Perhaps this is just a technical mistake. This is not about the Chief of Staff. I think that in peacetime this was done on the proposal of the defence ministry, and otherwise it was the chief of the legal administration, not anyone else, because we are legal professionals and we had nothing to do with anyone else. So I think that's where the mistake is. The person that is in charge, that is the legal profession, the legal administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've already had evidence from someone else in this case that the appointment was by the president on the recommendation of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, during the army -- during the wartime you know the General Staff became the Supreme Command Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And here he's making reference to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command, and I was trying to determine if he knew whether Supreme Command was something different from Supreme Command Staff. But I think he can't help --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But he's now changing his evidence to say that the recommendation is from the defence ministry and not from the chief of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think he was referring to peacetime, Your Honour, and that's in paragraph 21 of his statement. It is the recommendation of the defence minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was suggesting we've had evidence to the opposite effect, that in peacetime it was on the recommendation of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was looking for clarification of that. You're quite sure it was the Ministry of Defence that recommended the appointment of prosecutors in a state of peace?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I put here on the recommendation of the minister. Let me just check, or rather, we can resolve this issue in the following way. It is quite clearly stipulated in the law who proposes the appointments and the replacements and the removals from office, both in war and in peacetime, so we can just refer to those legal provisions so I just can't see where we're heading with these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you and I together, Mr. Blagojevic. For about 20 months now I've been suggesting that's the way to do it, but we still hear evidence from people like you about areas that should be absolutely beyond doubt because they're provided for in official documents. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 28, sir, you mention the decree law on the application of the Law on Criminal Procedure during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would advise you that can be found in an Exhibit, 1D301 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say: "Pursuant to that criminal investigations are" -- it's translated as "are not conducted for crimes punishable for a sentence of up to ten years." And I read Article 9 to say that criminal investigations are not required for crimes punishable up to a sentence of ten years, is that right, during a state of war?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, but could you please show this to me, this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can look at Exhibit 1D301, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we need Article 9.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indictments may be filed without an investigation and without the approval of the investigative judge. The only reason why this provision is in, it's to make the proceedings more efficient, more expeditious, but it does have a legal force of course, but it is only implemented during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. In paragraph 30 you make reference to the decree on organization and work of the military prosecutor during a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Exhibit P2786 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in paragraph 31 you make a reference to the Yugoslav Army's security organs or military police organs may apprehend a member of the military caught in a criminal act subject to ex officio prosecution. Can you tell us what that means in that context, "subject to ex officio prosecution," if the crime poses a threat to lives or an important asset, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain, this is Article 64 of the Law on Military Courts and this means that the military police organs may arrest a person, a perpetrator of a crime, only if that person was found in the very commission of the act. If that person is killing somebody or something like that, this is when this person can be arrested. Not in any other case. So this is an exception, but it is stipulated in the Law on Military Courts and Article 64.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 32 you're talking about the Yugoslav Army Rules of Service in relation to when a subordinate may receive an order to do something that would constitute a violation of law. Do you know what kind of training, if any, was given to officers and soldiers about these particular provisions of the Rules of Service?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can give you my impression, I don't have any direct knowledge of that kind of training, but I know that every soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you don't have any --

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Just allow me, please. What I know is this: Every soldier has to undergo training, every military serviceman has to get acquainted with the obligations and rights he or she has as a soldier, and the main rule that is applied in the Army of Yugoslavia is the Rules of Service. That is the essence of it, the alpha and the omega.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as I recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to interfere, but just to clarify. The Rules of Service is P1085 in our electronic system, in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be allowed to assist you, P1309, Article 27 -- Article 37, the state of war, the Law on Military Prosecutor's Offices will tell you who is in power to do what, that's at page 9 -- Article 9, page 9 in e-court, and that would make things clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's -- now there are three possibilities for us to look at and we will look at them all. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to P1085, I think it's page 28 of the English and page 37 of the B/C/S. Sir, I want to look to the items you mentioned dealing with the situation when a subordinate receives an order that might constitute a violation of law. And I hope we'll have it up on the screen here in a minute. In your statement you mention Articles 39 and 40, but I believe it may be Articles 38 and 39 because Article 40 seems to deal with carrying and use of a weapon --

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes -- well, it's obviously a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And if a soldier receives an order that would represent a violation of law, then the soldier is supposed to request that that order be given to him in writing; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but not only a soldier. Every serviceman, non-commissioned officers, officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. You're right. I meant to use it in the generic sense. And Article 39 says if someone receives such an order he or she should immediately inform a higher superior or somebody senior to the person who issued such an order; correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that relating you to the prosecution that you were involved in of Colonel Vukovic regarding the incitement to falsify official records regarding the fuel in the vehicles, in that situation the officer who actually made the entry in the official document, should he have reported it to Colonel Vukovic's superior under this provision, just so I understand how it works?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this provision has less legal weight than the criminal code, and it cannot automatically apply. Rules of Service are lower in the legal hierarchy in terms of their legal force, and the events that you are talking about, they are dealt with in the criminal procedure. But allow me to clarify. This provision has a bearing on disciplinary proceedings, if we're talking about this kind of a situation. So it's a completely different thing. In accordance with the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia and the Rules of Service for the same incident - allow me please - it is possible to have a cumulative proceedings, both criminal proceedings and disciplinary proceedings vis-a-vis the same act, the same incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll talk about that after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If that's agreeable, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We need to break again, Mr. Blagojevic. Could you again leave the courtroom, please, with the usher, and we will see you again at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Judge Kamenova will be absent this afternoon for urgent personal reasons. We have decided it's in the interests of justice that we should continue in her absence, which we will do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, we were just talking about the Rules of Service and the issue about a subordinate's alternatives when presented with an order that might constitute a violation of a law. I want to ask you in connection with Colonel Vukovic's case on which you were the prosecutor, did you attend the trial of that matter or did you conduct that trial?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I was the prosecuting attorney, so I was not in charge of the trial, I was not the presiding judge, but I did participate in the trial as the prosecuting attorney.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware or do you recall Colonel Vukovic ever saying in the course of the proceedings that he had done what he did after speaking with his superior officer, who he told us he thought was Colonel Stojiljkovic, and he did what he did because the Colonel had told him to do that? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't recall that, but could you please perhaps show me the case file because I can't really talk about in this way. I don't recall every single detail. I know just the key points. I can tell you what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well let me ask you this: If you had that information that his superior had ordered him to do that, wouldn't that have been a cause to open a case and investigate Colonel Stojiljkovic?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course a case should be opened against Colonel Stojiljkovic if that is what he did, but I don't really know that now. But proceedings should be instituted against him, but then the final decision would be made later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you don't recall having initiated any proceedings against Colonel Vukovic's superior in connection with that matter, do you?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the case file you can see that I did not do so. That means that I did not have this knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In your statement in paragraph 33 you're talking about the -- some provisions of the Law on the Army of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which, Your Honours, is Exhibit P984 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- regarding procedures and jurisdiction with respect to disciplinary responsibility. I'm curious about the phrasing. You say: "We wish to point out that Articles 159 and 206," et cetera. Who's the "we" you're referring to in this statement? Are you talking about you and Mr. Cepic or you and Mr. Petrovic? Those are the two guys who interviewed you. This is your statement. Why are you saying "we"?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is customary for the prosecutor to use the "we," so this is perhaps just unfortunate wording, but this is a reference to me. I am simply presenting to the Court that there are some disciplinary measures and some measures for the restitution of property that have bearing on the criminal proceedings because let me repeat once again, under our law it is possible to file cumulative charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand your answer then, and I would note that in paragraphs 43 and 46 and 47 you did use the personal pronoun "I." In paragraph 34 you are talking about these different procedures, and if I understand correctly it seems like there are three levels or three different means of handling discipline. There are disciplinary matters that can be handled by the superior officer, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I see Mr. Cepic on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to clear any dilemmas about the previous question. In our language the difference between the first person singular and first person plural is in one letter only, so this might be just a typo or technical issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One level at which the disciplinary matters can be handled is by the superior officer, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more clarification. There are two kinds of disciplinary responsibility, disciplinary error, this is something that is dealt with by the superior officer, but there are serious infractions of military discipline, disciplinary infractions or violations, and the military disciplinary court deals with those cases. In this case that would be the -- such a court at the 3rd Army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I understand correctly, military disciplinary courts are something different from the regular military courts that we've been talking about before now?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are those ad hoc courts that are set up just to deal with a particular case or are they permanent?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps this is again unfortunate wording, but I think that I did quote the appropriate articles, 159 through 194. These are not ad hoc courts. These are regular courts that exist in peacetime, in wartime, they exist right now, they are set up in accordance with the law. But perhaps now their a subject matter and territorial jurisdiction may be different, but this is very important for military discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who sits on these courts? Who are were judges?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. The president of the court is a military serviceman who does not have the appropriate qualifications but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, the -- you're speaking rather quickly for the interpreter. Could you start that answer again, please. Who were the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The presidents of military disciplinary courts are professional soldiers, so they are not lawyers. They do not have the appropriate professional knowledge. But registrars and prosecutors are professionals, lawyers, they are also military servicemen but they have a law degree. And let me just add, a new act is being drafted now and the courts will become professionalised, and this brings to the fore the importance of those institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to this, in paragraph 55 you mention the number of criminal reports that were filed which you say about 492 were for violations of international humanitarian law. And can you tell us what kinds of crimes fall under your definition of international humanitarian law. Does that include theft and theft of vehicles as well as robbery, rape, murder?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, the most serious crimes and then crimes of robbery against life and limb, rapes, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you do include theft and theft of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Theft -- let me just explain. Under our criminal law we have the institution of aggravated theft, the article is 166, paragraph 6 or 7, when the injured party is not identified. This is an aggravated theft, it may be aggravated because the person is an invalid or something like that or because it was done in the war or in special circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So do you include regular theft, non-aggravated theft, among your list of possible violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, probably. I can't now answer this question off the cuff without the documents, but probably yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And related to theft, in your direct testimony you mention -- I think you have a crime of petty theft, correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What's the maximum penalty for that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Up to three years, as far as I can recall, for petty theft.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for regular theft?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Three years in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for regular theft?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Regular theft carries the penalty of five years, and there's aggravated theft, Article 166, the -- it carries the penalty of up to ten years, and then we have robbery, armed robbery, and so on, where the penalties are much higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And for the three levels of theft that you just told us about, what distinguishes them? Does it have to do with the amount of property taken or does it have to do with the way in which the property is taken or does it have to do with who the victims are or some combination of those factors? Can you tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, lawyers cannot make their decision based on who the victims are. The law stipulates the way in which this is to be done. There are also qualifications and the value of what has been stolen. For instance, in one of those articles you have the provision that would be above 500.000 dinars, something like that, but there are a number of circumstances that have to be taken into account, time, place, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. These crimes that you described as falling under international humanitarian law, for example, a regular theft under some circumstances, could that be pursued as a disciplinary command -- disciplinary matter by the superior officer?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is a provision -- I don't want to paraphrase it, but it's Article 239 of the Criminal Code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, stipulating in detail that for less-severe crimes the perpetrators may not incur criminal proceedings, but they could be punished with disciplinary measures. But if you showed me this article then I would be able to point you to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What I'm trying to find out is if certain kinds of crimes that could be treated as war crimes could also be handled in the military disciplinary courts or as disciplinary matters under the jurisdiction of a superior officer. Was that possible?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I've already told you, and what I said was true. At the same time a military serviceman can be tried before a disciplinary court for disciplinary proceedings and criminal proceedings for any act, for all the acts where the military courts have jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in the system I'm familiar with, we have the principle of estoppel or res judicata. How would that work in your system with these three different levels if a soldier was prosecuted in the military disciplinary court for a particular theft, could he also be prosecuted in the criminal court later for the same event? Or would the military court be barred because that matter had already been adjudicated in the military disciplinary court?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: At one point the interpretation was interrupted so I didn't hear all of it, but I have understood the essence of what you were saying and I will respond. Lesser crimes that are referred to have adequate provisions. When the prosecutor decides, or rather, the prosecuting office, if they think that it is not necessary to bring criminal charges but to take disciplinary action, then that is what is done. But when I say "cumulatively," I mean that a military person can be held responsible in terms of being criminally responsible and responsible from a disciplinary point of view. And then of course we have to look at the significance of the crime committed and the danger for society and so on, so even -- if disciplinary measures are sufficient for meeting the purpose of the punishment, then that suffices.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And would the military prosecutor be a person who would make that decision about whether further prosecution was necessary after someone had already been prosecuted for a military disciplinary matter?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor's decision is autonomous, that is to say that the disciplinary proceedings decision cannot have an effect. But it is the autonomous decision of the prosecutor, whether he is going to initiate proceedings or not, it is his decision. I told you why, the importance of the case involved and the danger for society and so on. But as for crimes that entail imprisonment of over three years, then action is certainly taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You explained to us how when somebody in the military has been indicted and they have cases pending against them, when he's demobilised then the military court no longer has jurisdiction, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I don't know for what reasons. There is jurisdiction if a decision is made and if such a case is adjudicated then the military department does have jurisdiction in terms of rehabilitation on the basis of the law or if there is re-trial and so on because the person in question committed the crime in that previous capacity but then also other measures can be taken. For example, clearing the record and so on, but it's the military department that is asked and it is the district court that decides on such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But the military courts lose jurisdiction and those cases are transferred to the district courts; that's how I understood your answer before. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The translation of that last answer doesn't really make any sense in English, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm -- that's why I'm trying to follow-up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you understand my most recent question?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I understood, but let me just inform you of something, again this is a question that has to do with the law, it's a professional question. Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts regulates the way in which, or rather, when the indictment enters into legal force, who is in charge. But the point is that the prosecutor no longer has jurisdiction. It is the court that has jurisdiction. They either say that they do have jurisdiction or that they do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At what moment in time does that loss of jurisdiction occur? Is it the moment that a conscript is demobilised? Is it the moment the war is declared at an end? When is that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It depends on the stage of the proceedings involved, if an investigation is underway or the pre-trial proceedings, and this person then has a different capacity then the case is transferred to another court. If a person is no longer a military person and if there is an indictment against that person before a military court, in accordance with Article 13 of the Law on Military Courts then it is that court that tries that person, although that person no longer has the capacity of a military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So is the key then whether an indictment has been returned before the person is demobilised? In that situation can the military keep that person and try their case even though they're no longer a member of the army?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: We are probably not understanding each other. I don't know what you mean "has been returned." Once the indictment became final, entered into legal force, then the essence is that there was no challenge to the indictment, or rather, it could have been challenged but this was the ultimate decision taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, the reason I ask is I'm looking at an exhibit that is P954, this is a report dated the 20th of August, 2001, signed by Judge Colonel Miladinovic about the work of the military court in Nis and it lists, oh, a couple hundred cases. And many of them it shows what happened is the case -- the court no longer had jurisdiction and the case was transferred to the district court. Sometimes the date is not reflected when that occurred, but the dates vary from as early as I think July 15th, 1999, to as late as June of 2001. My question is, for example, with that case that's transferred in 2001, why has that taken so long to be transferred to the civilian court? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. How should I put this? The state of war gravely impeded the work of the prosecutor's office and of the courts. If there were that many complaints, can you imagine how much work there was to be done after the war? We would work from 7.00 a.m. until 7.00 p.m. even 8 p.m. Well, in all fairness I cannot see this report written by Miladinovic, the one that you referred to, but it probably pertains -- well, I cannot go into all the details, it wasn't presented to me that way, but perhaps it pertains to the stages that I mentioned, investigation, criminal report, and other evidence. As for the charges, I think that is quite clear and that I've already explained that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, let me show you just one example and maybe you can help me. In English it's page 53 of Exhibit 954, and I'll try and get you a hard copy, sir, because that may be easier to work from. This is -- if I could have the usher -- I'm sorry, my B/C/S page is not matching up. The translation doesn't appear to be consistent across the page. I'll read this entry to you, and then I'll try and find the page for the record, but it involves indictments filed in the military court in Nis, and it involves an indictment against an individual named Radoslav Lazarevic for an alleged crime on the 19th of May, 1999, he's charged with Article 166, stealing a tractor and trailer. And the proceedings were initiated in May of 2000. He's a reserve private. And then in August of 2001 there's a finding of absence of jurisdiction and it's handed over to the municipal court. Do you know why that case would have been started against a reserve private in 2000, almost a year after the war was over, and yet it takes another year to determine that jurisdiction should be transferred to the civilian court?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an answer to that, but I assume that first of all the objection to this indictment -- well, actually, that a decision was not made with regard to the challenge to this indictment, that is to say that it did not enter into legal force. But if I'm telling you -- well, a year's time, I don't know what the overall number of cases is, but as for wartime cases are concerned, also cases from the case load of the military prosecutor, well I told you there were a great many of those and I told you how we worked and there were probably priorities, these were very important cases. I really don't know, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And one last document I want to ask you about is P1011. This is Ivan Markovic's document that you refer to in your statement: "The application of rules of international law of armed conflicts." One reference you made is that commission that went to Istok that you were a part of, you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
