utterances.text: And do you recall that group of Siptar refugees that were in the school there, do you recall that they reported that earlier they had been trying to travel towards Albania and they had been robbed by a group of armed uniformed men I think -- you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I do. That was the statement made by these persons. I remember this other statement of those same persons. I don't know what the exact number was, I wasn't the chairman of the commission, I was involved in a completely different line of work. I know that they were taken care of by the army and that they were provided everything that they needed at that point in time and in that situation in terms of their food, accommodation, and so on. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was any investigation started to try and locate the perpetrators of that robbery that took place against those people?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do not have knowledge to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: But that can be checked probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to that event -- well, it was presented. And then after that, measures could have been taken but I don't know if measures were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Because -- well, it was really for the military police to act in accordance with this to see whether these allegations were correct or not and to see who the perpetrators were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I want to refer you to a report that's contained in that document, it's at English page 164 and in the B/C/S I think it's page 119, if my note is correct. This is a report from the military prosecutor in Nis dated the 6th of April, 2001, to the 3rd Army command. And it's called: "Information on criminal proceedings for crimes committed in Kosovo and Metohija." I'm not sure we have the right B/C/S page. Have you tried page number 110 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While I'm trying to locate that page for you, I wanted to ask you about the numbers you reported of international humanitarian crimes. Do you know what percentage of that number in your statement involved crimes against life and limb?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we just have a look and see whether I signed this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I'm not asking you about the report right now. In your statement at paragraph 55 you mention --

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: 55, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. You mentioned 2.382 reports and 492 for violations of international humanitarian law. Of those 492 how many involved crimes against life and limb?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you an answer to that. I told you it was almost a fifth of the reported crimes, but I really cannot know because I was not in a position to know what the number was. I am speaking in tentative terms on the basis of the knowledge that I had and on the basis of what was written down. How many, well it must have been over a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And how many of those resulted in convictions?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, if we are talking about very serious crimes, 98 per cent were convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you now the page in B/C/S on the screen, this is that report from the military prosecutor in Nis that's in Markovic's publication. You recall ever seeing this document?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Please show it to me. I can't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you see the page? On the left under 3rd Army command?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "We hereby inform you that in the period between 1 March 1998 and today," which is dated the 6th of April, 2001, they talk about a total of 245 persons for criminal acts committed in Kosovo between 1 March NATO and 26 June 1999. Do you follow that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that such reports are reserved for the military prosecutor. And really, I do not recall having seen this. I can confirm that while I was at the command of the Pristina Corps that I gave reports on the number of judgements, et cetera, but obviously this is not written in that style.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you'll see --

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I allow for the possibility that this is a correct report. I'm not saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, this is page 110 of the B/C/S. You'll see it indicates of that number of 245, 183 were charged. An investigation was still in progress against 47, and for 15 others information was being collected. Of the 47 persons charged, it appears that only six of those were for crimes involving life and limb, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I see it from the report, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we go to page 3 of the English and it's on page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This must be a mistake. Of the how many charged it appears only six were for crimes involving life and limb --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Of the 47 persons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought 183 were charged and investigation was still in progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke, Your Honour, for the investigations in progress against 47, six were for crimes against life and limb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 111 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the very bottom of --

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Allow me, please, Mr. President. With your permission, this has to do with 183 indicted persons. Could you please return the document again, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, just you listen to the question, please, Mr. Blagojevic. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to try to deal with that, Mr. Blagojevic. On page 111 you should see a reference to that number that you were just talking about. At the bottom of page 165 in English it says the charges against 182 persons. I assume that's a typo and it should mean 183, as it said in the beginning. Of those 182 charged it said crimes resulting in death or other consequences to life and limb and crimes of personal moral degradation against 13 persons and crimes against citizens' property 169. So out of the 182 or 183, only 13 were for crimes involving life and limb; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness cannot see this document in front of him because in the Serbian version, or rather, B/C/S it is not on the screen. So could that please be done so that the witness could answer the question that is being put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we have to scroll all the way to the bottom, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You see in the right-hand column near the lower quarter of the page the reference to the 182 persons? Yes.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see only 13 out of that 182 or 183 who were charged were charged with crimes involving life and limb; the rest were property crimes, right?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this report is correct and my information was tentative. I really was not in a position to have the exact data. The military prosecutor absolutely does have such data available.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, then how is it you come in here and tell us that there were 492 violations of international humanitarian law? Where do you get that number from?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: It's a tentative figure. It is the report of the military court attached to the command of Pristina Corps and the command of the military district. It's based on the register, and taking into account - how should I put this? - all these cases, thefts, rapes, and so on, almost a fifth of what I said pertains to that figure. I don't have very precise information because a great deal of analysis is required for that. How many reported, how many investigations, how many trials, how many judgements, how many convictions, so this is not a precise figure; it is of a tentative nature. One-fifth of the perpetrators of crimes who were reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, how is your number in 2008 a tentative number compared to this number from 2001? And you had access to this document. You referred to pages 69 and 70 in your statement of this document?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Where do I mention this report?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't mention this report. You mention this document, Markovic's document, or did you only look at the two pages that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Where did I mark that? In what paragraph do I refer to this, in what paragraph of my statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 42 of your statement you mention page 67 of the second edition of Markovic's publication, application of the international law of war."

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you want to say, Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say something regarding paragraph 42. I did say that it was published in this book, the -- that the instructions what soldiers have to do in a war, how to treat the prisoners, and so on, this was why I included this in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but Mr. Hannis is making the point to you that the document to which we've been referred, the report by the military in Nis, is also in that volume. So why did you not take that into account in preparing your material for this court is his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't do that because that was not my task, but it would require a comprehensive analysis of the data and I only provided rough data, tentative data.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, for the record I need to indicate two other things. When I was reading from Exhibit P954, the B/C/S page regarding Private Lazarevic is page 50 in e-court of Exhibit 954. And there's a second reference to Markovic's book in the witness's statement at paragraph 69. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, before the war there was a system of military courts and, therefore, military prosecutors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And for the area that we're concerned with, were they based in Nis at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there must have been a number of experienced prosecutors there?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the war I can't talk about that because I was not a member, so I have very little knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm curious to know why none of them was instantly appointed to the posts in Pristina, but you with no experience at all were appointed there.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you any other answer but the following. That was my misfortune. It was a difficult job and I had to do it in accordance with the orders, so I can't really answer why I did that. You have to ask my superiors who actually stipulated all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is it as easy as that? Were you not surprised?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had to accept the appointment I was given. I was not surprised because I had the most experienced lawyers in this unit where I was, so this was the easiest part because I didn't make decisions just like that. I consulted the collegium. But as to what led them to make this appointment, this is not something that I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you didn't say, Why me?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer you. Perhaps it was maybe fear for some part. I really can't give you that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you held the post of prosecutor briefly, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean when I was working?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were military prosecutor at the beginning of the war, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Colonel Stanimir Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: During the war he was the president of the department of the supreme military prosecutor's office headquartered in Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do have a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, I have just a couple of questions for you. My learned colleague Mr. Hannis and the Presiding Judge mentioned the issue of your appointment and your previous experience. What I wanted to know is the following: Your deputies in the prosecutor's office, did they have experience in this kind of work, prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can say that my deputies had the most experience, the highest qualifications, because, for instance, Djordje Aksic had been the justice minister in Kosovo and Metohija; Dragoljub Zdravkovic had been a judge for over 20 years and he dealt with the most serious crimes; Miodrag Brkic was the district prosecutor for a long time, he had more than 20 years of experience; Momcilo Dedic, and so on. I think that he had over 15 years of prosecutorial experience at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The other judges and prosecutors at the Pristina Corps command and the command of the military district in Pristina, did they have the same kind of experience as Zoran Saveljic?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. But Zoran Saveljic was at a different court, the military court at the Pristina Corps command and Miladinovic was the president of that court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The experienced colleagues that you mentioned, were they active-duty servicemen before the war in the military?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no. The only military persons performing these tasks were Sasa Boskovic, Miladinovic, Zdravkovic, and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This may be a leading question. Does that mean that all the deputies and all the judges that were part of that court were lawyers with a great deal of experience who actually reported as reserve officers?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already explained. They did not report, but they had to report, they had to respond to the call-up when the military court was set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that before the war they knew that they had their assignment as reserve officers there?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, we talked about the proceedings against Colonel Vlatko Vukovic. My learned colleague Mr. Hannis painted the picture for you, a hypothetical situation, what would have happened had Colonel Vukovic received an order from his superior; and you gave your answer. What I'm interested in is: What would have happened had Vukovic merely informed his superior about that?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really can't give you an answer to this kind of question. These are hypothetical questions. I can't tell you what would have happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. That's not what Vukovic said he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That misstates the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the factual basis for that proposition, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely this, because I am almost 100 per cent sure that Colonel Vukovic did say that he had informed his superior, not that he had received an order from his superior. I did not want to object to that during the examination by Mr. Hannis. We can either check the transcript or even listen to the tapes if it was perhaps wrongly recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you it's not my recollection of the evidence, no one interrupted at the time, and in any event the witness has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the transcript at 21454, line 10, is pertinent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, we saw a document dated the 6th of April, 2001, and it pertained, if I am not mistaken in my recollection, to persons who were reported and who were identified by their name. Could you please look at paragraph 55 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You state here in the second sentence that almost one-fifth of all the criminal reports were filed for violations of international humanitarian law, 492 criminal reports. My question: Can a criminal report be filed against unidentified perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, but there has to be an additional clarification. In accordance with the Law on Criminal Procedure, if the perpetrator of a crime is unidentified the prosecutor is authorised to carry out the following actions. He may ask the military police to carry out certain investigative measures to identify the perpetrator of a crime, that's one of the options. Another option is to -- to address the competent military court and to request that certain investigative measures be taken. And then the court will rule on this request or proposal. But if the court dismisses such a request, the investigative judge will then present the proposal before the KV council and they have the authority to make the final decision whether those investigative measures will be taken or not. And then the court of course will order that certain measures be taken, such as, for instance, post mortem examinations and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Let us be very specific here. Did you personally receive criminal reports against unidentified perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and let me explain --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But could you please be very brief.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: For terrorist acts and conspiracy, for hostile acts involving multiple victims among soldiers --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is one of the crimes, but, for instance, when you would have soldiers who committed suicide and so on, then the measures I mentioned are taken in order to shed light on to this event to see who did what and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And as for the mass graves, we mentioned them today, the initial criminal report, who is it filed against at the very first moment if you don't know anything?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you don't know the perpetrator that would be the unidentified perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel and witness please make pauses between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: We saw some criminal reports for violations of international humanitarian law involving unidentified perpetrators, so that is my question, thefts, robberies, and so on.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, naturally we saw that such reports existed then decisions were taken on those reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could I have a reference to where we saw unidentified perpetrators for thefts and robberies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you look at 5D -- or P954 and P955 we have a clear indication that unidentified perpetrators are reported for the most serious of crimes, and when we talked about the mass graves in the Slovinje and Mali Alas again we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please concentrate on the question. You're being asked for a citation for unidentified perpetrators of crimes against property.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not until you tell us the place where we can find material of unidentified perpetrators of crimes against property. Is it the same exhibits or is it a different exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't claim that with any certainty. I have to go through all the material that I have at my disposal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but I'm certain for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. You've made the point, Mr. Hannis. It will be checked. Mr. Cepic, I hope we're nearing the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question by your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, after the 6th of April, 2001, were any crimes detected in Kosovo and Metohija and were they investigated and were other measures taken to shed light on those crimes?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, who would commit those crimes?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, crimes committed by military personnel.

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if there were some incidents in 1999 some would come to light in ten days and some three or four years after the incident. That was not something that was up to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: After this report that was dated the 6th of April, 2001, the one that was shown to you by the prosecutor, the report from Nis from the -- from Stanimir Radosavljevic, military prosecutor from Nis, were any new investigations launched after this report?

utterances.speaker: DJURA BLAGOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the information to tell you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Blagojevic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to assist us. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, do we recognise you for the next witness? MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, our next witness is Dr. Aleksandar Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Petkovic, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Petrovic on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. M. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Dr. Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Aleksandar Petkovic. I was born on the 24th of November, 1950, in the village of Hum, near Nis. My father's name is Sekula; my mother's name is Milutinka.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's enough. Did you give a statement to General Lazarevic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Were you able to read this statement and to sign it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same -- those questions, would you give the same answers that you gave in your statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this statement as 5D1403.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Doctor, what is your occupation now?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I am the chief of the surgery department in the military hospital in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did you work in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 I worked in the surgery department of the military hospital in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraph 3 you say that in 1998, in addition to VJ soldiers, captured and wounded KLA members were also treated in the military hospital in Nis?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please wait a moment for me to finish my question. And could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: I claim that in 1998 and 1999 the surgery department of the Nis military hospital treated the captured KLA members who had been wounded. Their wounds were of such a nature, they were such extensive wounds, that they required lengthy or complex treatment; and that is why they were sent to Nis to the surgery department of the Nis military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you keep records of that in the military hospital in Nis?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did keep records. For each person that was examined there are valid medical records, persons who were examined and treated appropriately and who did not require hospitalisation were entered in the relevant protocols at the surgery department, and all those who were hospitalised had their medical files opened and all the relevant documents were placed inside those files. And I can say that the wounded KLA members who were treated in the Nis military hospital received absolutely the same treatment, medical treatment, as did VJ military personnel and all the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Could we please have 4D519 up on our screens. Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not aware that we got notification that this document was going to be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, we did put it through the IC and it was actually tendered by General Pavkovic's Defence, so that was admitted into evidence as their exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The point being made is that this was not on your list of exhibits to be referred to in your examination. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I have to check that with our case manager, but I do think that it was announced, it was notified, and I see that my colleague Mr. Aleksic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to know why. Yes, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, I think that my colleagues from General Lazarevic's Defence did not have a translation of this document. They had it under a different number but it was not translated, but in order to make everyone's lives easier we told them that we had the same document with a CLSS translation. And as far as I know, they did notify it under a 5D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the 5D number to satisfy Ms. Carter? MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] That was 5D1413.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I did receive notification of that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not only that, you're now getting the English translation as well, for which I'm sure you are even more grateful. Mr. Petrovic. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Dr. Petkovic, could you please look at this document, and could you please tell us whether this is the list that you were telling us about a little while ago, that these are the records that you kept, and could you please comment on it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the list. This is the list of the injured terrorists or KLA members who were treated at the surgery department of the Nis military hospital. I would like to stress that we don't have to analyse each and every case, but I focused on two and by your leave I can comment --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me just give you one example, Enver Krasniqi - and I have his medical history here with me, perhaps we can see it, it contains all the documents that were produced at the surgery department - he had a gun-shot wound to his right shin and explosive wounds to his left --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Petkovic, it's for Mr. Petrovic to ask you the questions he wants to ask you. How exactly this particular person was treated doesn't strike me as something we need to know about in the course of this trial. So just wait until a question's asked before you embark upon an answer. Mr. Petrovic. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Dr. Petkovic, in paragraph 4 of your statement you said that several times during the course of 1998 and 1999 you were in Kosovo and Metohija. In whose composition were you while you were in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1998 it wasn't only me but the entire surgical team from the military hospital was engaged in the military garrison of Djakovica. At that time I was in Djakovica twice, namely, in July and October and November respectively. We worked at the garrison infirmary that is within the garrison of Djakovica. We turned it into a surgery clinic. We established it ourselves, and in such difficult conditions we tried to help those who were wounded and who were sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me briefly, what was the organization of the medical corps like in the Pristina Corps in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: You put this question a moment ago, and I didn't manage to answer. The teams that worked worked in the garrison of Djakovica were under the immediate command of the Pristina Corps, or rather, General Lazarevic. As for the organization of the medical corps in Kosovo and Metohija, I can say the following. In the Pristina Corps it was organized according to the system --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: It was organized according to the principle of the medical corps tactics that were in force at the time and the medical battalion was there, Colonel Disic was its commander with two medical companies that were deployed in the broader area of Podujevo. Also, every brigade had mobilised its own medical company, specialists, surgeons, internists, psychiatrists, and many others worked in these medical companies, not to go into all of the details. However, all of these medical companies that were working there were located closer to the front line, or rather, the actual war developments, in order to help the wounded out in the field as best possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, in these infirmaries in Kosovo and Metohija, in Djakovica and Kosovska Mitrovica, who was treated there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Djakovica infirmary it was primarily the wounded from the Army of Yugoslavia and the wounded terrorists who were taken prisoner. At the medical centre of Prizren and the medical centre of Kosovska Mitrovica, that are hospitals in actual fact, and also in 1999 our teams were there. In addition to members of the Army of Yugoslavia, captured members of the KLA were treated there, as was the civilian population of all ethnic backgrounds living in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: When you're speaking about members of the KLA, is that what you actually say in paragraph 7 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's precisely what I have in mind. Captured members of the KLA were brought to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we understand the point; it's in your statement. Is there a similar document showing the identities of all these people treated in Djakovica, the same as in Nis? MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we going to see it? MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour. We have a list of the terrorists, the captured KLA members, who were treated in Djakovica as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] It's under the same number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you intending to present it to the witness or are you -- MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour. 5D1413.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, 5D1413 was the document that I was given notification of. I was told that 4D519 is in fact the same document, that's where we got the English translation. Unfortunately, looking at 4D519 which has been presented to the Court right now, it actually includes an additional page that wasn't provided to us under 5D1413. We have an objection to the first page of 4D519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why? Is it going to cause you real problem of some kind or -- or are you just objecting for the sake of objecting? Give me a basis for this objection. I know it's a technical breach of the rule, but is there some good solid reason why you're objecting?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need to fully investigate what the entire document is. I am just getting print-outs right now. However, we were not given notification of it. And from a cursory glance of it, it also indicates that there's an attachment of an additional 12 pages that's nowhere in either document. So it seems there's some underlying material and some problems with this exhibit that we were not provided with full documentation on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But the problem is the one that's being used is 5D1413 and 4D519 was only used for the purpose of giving you an English translation. It's been exhibited, though, in a different connection and presumably the whole of it is part of the evidence in the case; although, I can't be sure as things stand at the moment. How do we get into these ridiculous messes in this case almost two years down the line. We are trying to get through your witnesses help them to get back to their own -- these are doctors who are needed, and the last place on earth they want to be is sitting in a court or sitting in The Hague for the weekend while patients wait unattended. Now, what's your explanation for not giving the full information to Ms. Carter? I think the next witness runs the department -- the whole establishment as I understand it, and we've got a sitting around here kicking our heels. Why are they here at all, in fact? Why is all of this not all done in writing to save the expertise of these very valuable people where it's really needed? It's almost scandalous to bring, you know, people like that here just -- I don't know for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me, if I understand Rule 92 ter correctly, in addition to the statement the content of the statement has to be confirmed by the witnesses who have to be brought in; otherwise, if we could have just tendered the statements on their own we wouldn't have brought the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you tried to reach agreement -- one of the duties that you're supposed to undertake in this court is to reach agreement with the Prosecution about things to save this, and 92 bis is the rule you then use. You don't need cross-examination. What effort did you make to reach agreement on this evidence, Mr. Petrovic? MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we tendered this and it just has to do with lists of persons. We just wanted to demonstrate that as our witness stated in paragraph 7, the list contains captured KLA terrorists who were treated in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. Well, we will repel the objection for the sake of making progress here. If it causes prejudice to the Prosecution, we will ignore this evidence if it can be shown that you haven't followed the Rules. But the evidence will be before us so we can make use of it. If you don't finish both witnesses this afternoon, we will not hear the other witness; she [sic] will go back and get on with her proper duties rather than spend her time here, so make up your mind how you're going to deal with this. MR. M. PETROVIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to be very brief. Just one more question for this witness. Actually, that will do, Your Honours. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any Defence cross-examination? No. Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No cross-examination from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Petkovic, that completes your evidence. I'm extremely sorry you've had to be brought here at all, and I understand you may have been waiting as well to give evidence. It seems to us quite unnecessary that your duties should have been disrupted in this way, and I'm sorry we have a system where no effort appears to have been made to reach agreement on your evidence in a way that would have avoided inconveniencing you. Thank you for being here. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our next witness, Your Honour, is Dr. Ivica Milosavljevic. And, if you allow me, while we're waiting for the witness, Your Honour, I may be making a mistake but since we objected to the 92 bis statements of the OTP it was stated at the very beginning that in principle they would file an objection too. So we really didn't discuss that and we really, therefore, can perhaps explain it by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we've still a few more witnesses in this case and I hope note is being taken of the concern expressed by the Bench of bringing here witnesses when no effort has been made to try to reach agreement on their evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not sure whether you meant the Defence that follows. We just have this 92 bis witness and yet another one and that would complete our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, your next one apparently is live and unless you're going to change the situation at the weekend -- is that not the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This witness, Ivica Milosavljevic, is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think -- well, I'll try -- actually, first I'll ask you to give me the time I asked for for that witness, and I think that it's going to be shorter than the time I had envisaged. However, the statement and the translation will lead to a problem; namely, that Mr. Hannis cannot be made aware of it on time. So perhaps it should be a live witness, but I will do my best to shorten the time involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the moment you've programmed that witness for two days, and that's a matter of concern to us. He must be awfully important at this stage in your case to be programmed for that length of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, four hours is what I envisaged and I think I can do with three hours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Four hours in this court is two days. The mistake --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- made so often is to ignore the fact that it's the time spent by others, other than the one leading the witness, that actually takes up most of our time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a very important witness who was mentioned often. You also asked about that witness, that is, the chief of the operative organ in the Pristina Corps. Perhaps he could have testified today as well. I don't want this to sound as if I were criticising the Prosecution, but we had a longer cross-examination of a few witnesses this week than had been originally envisaged and I think that contributed to the fact that we are running late today in terms of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I need to start, Dr. Milosavljevic, with an apology to you. I had in earlier discussions in the course -- in the court mistaken your gender. The second thing we need to do is for you to make the solemn declaration to speak the truth. Could you do that, please, by reading aloud the document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You'll now be examined by Mr. Bakrac on behalf of Mr. Lazarevic. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Milosavljevic, for the purposes of the record, could you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm Dr. Ivica Milosavljevic, a specialist in forensic medicine, and now I am head of the centre for pathology and forensic medicine and at the same time the head of the forensic medicine institute that is part of this centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the 11th of January, 2008, you made a statement to the Defence of General Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: If we were to ask you the same questions today, would you give us the same answers as you did in making your statement?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that is 5D1404, and I would like to tender it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Doctor, we are not going to repeat what the statement contains. I just have a few more additional questions. In paragraphs 5 and 6 you said that on the 27th of April -- on the 27th of April you came to Pristina in the afternoon and that you cannot remember exactly where it was that the driver took you. Was it the same afternoon and who was it that you saw in Pristina on that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the same afternoon since I did not go to Pristina often before that and I did not really know Pristina and the surrounding area, I just remember I was taken out of town, I was told it was the temporary command post, I was told it was the building of some mine and that is where I encountered General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosavljevic. In paragraph 12 you spoke about a meeting in respect of the clean-up of the terrain. Do you remember who chaired this meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was organized at the initiative of General Lazarevic, and he himself chaired the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, I would be interested in the following. As for these two localities where you carried out the post mortems, what methodology of procedure was applied?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Since we were working in the field and we had to deal with a large number of corpses, we conducted part of the forensic post mortem that is called external findings, which is allowed under such conditions. This is allowed in many international recommendations, protocols, and standards, the Minnesota Protocol and UN protocols in terms of actions taken by forensic pathologists in cases of torture and other forms of unlawful loss of life and documents related to the Council of Europe. All of this was confirmed in the beginning of February and the end of January 2003 at a consensus conference organized by the International Committee of the Red Cross, where clarifications were given in respect of the application of such procedures, like external findings, and also what is compulsory on such occasions so that this external examination would be of forensic significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosavljevic. I would be interested in Slovinje and Mali Alas, these two localities where you worked. Did you have contact with the families of exhumed persons?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Since one of the chief tasks in those circumstances is the identification of the persons who were killed, of course we had direct contact with the families and the families in fact assisted us based on our descriptions, the documents that we found, and their descriptions, and the direct process of identification by sight, that all helped us to identify those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosavljevic, the examinations that you carried out and the expert reports that you provided in writing, do you have any knowledge whether they were used to prosecute some people?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge, right now both cases are on trial before the district court in Belgrade before the war crimes chamber, and I saw in the media that UNPROFOR, or rather, UNMIK, that was in 2002 or 2003, I don't remember when it was that I heard that, instituted legal proceedings against the perpetrators of the crime in the village of Slovinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Milosavljevic: What do you know about the experience from other countries in armed conflict regarding such expert reports from the field of forensic medicine?

utterances.speaker: IVICA MILOSAVLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, not a lot has been published, but fortunately not many people in countries had to experience this. But we always strove, as I just explained when I talked about the standards that we applied, we always tried to deploy full teams with the highest degree of qualifications so that they can do their jobs as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosavljevic. And that is the last question. I don't have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Ms. Kravetz -- sorry. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness, Your Honour. I just wanted to point out one small detail with regard to an exhibit that's referred to in this witness's statement, it's 5D1316. The English translation of that exhibit does not correspond to the text of the B/C/S, there's an additional page which actually corresponds to a different exhibit, and we have alerted the Lazarevic Defence to this point so that can be corrected. And I just ask that that be admitted once that has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. That one will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to confirm that this is being corrected, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Milosavljevic, that completes your evidence here. I'm sorry that you have had to come here at all. We consider that this matter could have been dealt with without requiring your attendance, but as it is thank you for coming and assisting us. You are now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall adjourn now and resume here on Tuesday morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 5th day of February, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24
